Search all the findings and their sources

Our read: agents are multiplying faster than teams can coordinate them

This is our read of the evidence, and no public study has tested it yet. Nearly every team surveyed already uses AI, and Gartner expects agents to outnumber sellers 10 to 1 by 2028. The clearest reported gains come from companies that rebuilt a workflow around AI, measured it by the unit of work and redeployed the time it freed. We expect that doing this at scale takes two disciplines.

Agent enablement

Getting an agent ready to do a job well: a charter, the right context, instructions written from the best performer’s process, an evaluation set, a scorecard and review until the corrections stop. It is the lifecycle you already run for a new hire.

The enablement play

Orchestration

Coordinating many agents and people across the revenue process: one shared record, designed handoffs, approvals and escalation, a log of every step and unit costs measured across the whole workflow.

The orchestration play

What would change our read

Public evidence on orchestration is still thin. Most measured results come from single agents in single workflows, and most leader-versus-laggard gaps are associations.

Two preprints from autumn 2026 already cut against it, and neither has been peer reviewed. In a randomized trial on 100 websites, a single sales agent raised revenue per visitor by 10.0%, so one agent can produce a measured gain with no orchestration at all. In a controlled comparison across 13 enterprise-style procedures, coordinated agent designs used 1.4 to 4.7 times the tokens of a single agent with no overall gain in success. Neither tests live GTM work across a revenue process.

We will review this read by May 20, 2027, which is 6 months from this edition. We will review it sooner if a study of live GTM work appears. We will drop it if studies with a comparison group show coordinated agents costing more per verified completion than a single agent at the same quality, in lead handling, support escalation or renewal preparation. We will narrow it if single agents alone keep producing measured gains, as the website trial did. Evidence either way goes in the register.

Enable agents like new hires. Orchestrate the whole team.

AI and the Redefinition of GTM Work: Leaders, Laggards and the Evidence

Research report, revised November 20, 2026. Reviewed by its editor and by AI models; not peer reviewed.

AI is redefining go-to-market work, but the evidence of results is concentrated. The clearest reported gains come from companies that rebuilt a specific workflow around AI, measured it by the unit of work and redeployed the time it freed. Beyond those cases the record is mixed, not negative.

Read the reportSee what the revision changed

Eight findings

  1. Almost every team uses AI; a minority say it is ready.
  2. Where work has been rebuilt, companies report automation rates from above 30% to 91%, each on its own measure.
  3. Leaders and laggards differ sharply, but the comparisons are associations.
  4. The leaders’ common practice is redesign before automation.
  5. More service leaders report moving people than cutting them, and entry-level employment is weakening.
  6. Cutting on cost alone risks quality, though the best-known case is disputed.
  7. Most sales organizations report low reinvestment of the time AI saves.
  8. New roles are appearing.

Executive summary

AI is redefining go-to-market work, but the evidence of results is concentrated. The clearest reported gains come from companies that rebuilt a specific workflow around AI, measured it by the unit of work and redeployed the time it freed. Beyond those cases the record is mixed, not negative: BCG counts a further 41% of companies scaling AI and outperforming laggards, and a peer-reviewed field study of 5,172 support agents found that AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average. The surveys that compare leaders with laggards point to operating practice more than access to tools, but they show association, not cause.

Key findings

  1. Almost every team uses AI; a minority say it is ready. Both surveys behind this come from vendors. In Salesloft’s 2026 benchmark of 500 U.S. revenue leaders at companies with 200 or more employees, every respondent uses AI somewhere in the revenue process, but 20.6% describe it as production-ready with measurable outcomes. In LeanData’s customer survey of 157 GTM practitioners, 93% have deployed at least one AI agent, while 31% call their infrastructure ready and 63% somewhat ready.
  2. Where work has been rebuilt, companies report automation rates from above 30% to 91%, each on its own measure. The reported rates run from more than 30% of client requests resolved without a person to 91% of support tickets automated (Figure 2). Because each company counts differently, the rates are not comparable.
  3. Leaders and laggards differ sharply, but the comparisons are associations. In McKinsey’s 2026 B2B survey, 60% of market-share leaders grew revenue by double digits, against 21% of laggards. BCG’s 7.5% of “future-built” companies had 2.4 times the revenue growth and 2.8 times the EBITDA growth of laggards over 2022 to 2025, figures BCG takes from financial databases. Both studies group companies by performance or AI maturity, so neither shows that AI caused the gap.
  4. The leaders’ common practice is redesign before automation. Bain’s top performers and BCG’s future-built companies describe redesigning a workflow before automating it. In the peer-reviewed field study, less experienced support agents gained most from AI assistance, and its authors offer suggestive evidence that the tool spread the practices of more able agents. Building an agent from the best performer’s process is a practice worth testing, not a proven cause of growth.
  5. More service leaders report moving people than cutting them, and entry-level employment is weakening. In Gartner’s 2026 survey of 275 service and support leaders, 21% had reduced agent headcount because of AI. A larger share, 71%, were shifting agents into different roles within service and support. Gartner’s release ties only the headcount cut to AI. Stanford finds that employment of U.S. workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers.
  6. Cutting on cost alone risks quality, though the best-known case is disputed. Klarna’s CEO told Bloomberg in May 2025 that cost had weighed too heavily and quality had suffered, and Klarna began recruiting human agents. Klarna later told SEC staff that the remarks concerned a pilot of freelance customer experience consultants and that it runs AI and human support side by side. Its annual report for 2025 says the assistant handled 80% of customer service chats, with satisfaction on a par with human agents by Klarna’s own surveys. Gartner predicts that half of the companies that cut service staff because of AI will rehire by 2027.
  7. Most sales organizations report low reinvestment of the time AI saves. AI saves sellers 4.8 hours a week, yet 72% of sales organizations report low reinvestment of that time in high-value work (Gartner, 210 sales leaders).
  8. New roles are appearing. Salesforce has created roles such as AI conversation designer and forward-deployed engineer. Bloomberry, which sells job-postings data, counts GTM engineering and RevOps postings together and finds them up 205% in January to September 2025 against the same months of 2024, with SQL and Python each appearing in 38% of GTM-engineer postings.

Practices associated with leaders. Test each in your own data:

  • pick a few high-volume workflows;
  • write down the best performer’s process;
  • measure each unit of work against a comparison group;
  • keep people accountable for exceptions and money;
  • reinvest freed capacity on purpose;
  • build internal capability (GTM engineering, evaluation and governance) rather than collecting point tools.

What holds laggards back.

  • Data and process debt.
  • Tools layered onto unchanged workflows.
  • No plan for freed capacity.
  • Missing controls for agents.
  • Skills, roles and incentives that have not changed.

Where to start. Name three to five workflows, each with a single owner. Measure the baseline and keep a comparison group. Decide in advance where freed capacity goes, and what result, over what period, would justify scaling.

1. Scope, sources and method

This report examines what the public record shows about AI’s effect on go-to-market work, and what separates the companies reporting value from those that are not. It is written for chief revenue officers and for leaders of sales, marketing, customer success, support and revenue operations.

Dataset and range. The evidence base is the set of findings in Appendix A, drawn from four kinds of public material published between February 2024 and November 20, 2026. The data coverage note above explains what the Q3 2026 earnings season has not yet produced.

Source type Examples used here What it can show Main limitation
Filings and earnings calls Fiserv (November 3, 2026), HubSpot (November 4, 2026) Results stated under disclosure rules, sometimes in financial terms Rarely explains how the work changed; the Q3 season is still under way
Operator disclosures Fin (formerly Intercom; part of Salesforce since September 2026), Klarna, Salesforce, Shopify, Vercel, Zapier How a workflow was rebuilt, and what happened to the people Self-reported, often by companies that sell the tools; definitions change over time
Independent and academic research Gartner, BCG, McKinsey, Bain, two arXiv preprints, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, Quarterly Journal of Economics Patterns across many organizations, one peer-reviewed causal field study and two experiments that have not been peer reviewed Most surveys capture perception and compare groups chosen by outcome or maturity
Vendor and platform data Microsoft Work Trend Index, Gong, Salesforce State of Sales, LeanData, Salesloft, Seismic, Instantly, Bloomberry, ChurnZero Large datasets on specific GTM activities Vendors study their own users and often sell the remedy

Evidence grades. Each entry in Appendix A is graded on what it proves. The companion report on Q3 2026 earnings, still in review, uses the same grades:

  • A, financial: the effect is stated in financial terms, such as a cost saving, a return or a profit improvement.
  • B, measured: a quantified operating or labor-market result, such as a resolution rate, a headcount change or employment data, with no financial translation.
  • C, survey, forecast or narrative: perceptions, predictions, comparisons between groups or qualitative claims. A forecast or a target is C whatever its units, so a savings target stated in dollars is not graded A.

Each entry also states its basis: observed (measured in records or accounts), self-reported (a company or respondent describing its own results), estimated (a respondent’s or company’s estimate) or forecast.

Reading the numbers.

  • Most leader-versus-laggard gaps compare groups at one point in time, and several studies define the groups by the outcome itself, such as growth, margins or market share. They show association, not cause.
  • Companies define “resolved,” “contained,” “handled” and “automated” differently, and some changed their definitions during 2026. Rates are not like-for-like, and a trend needs one cohort and one definition.
  • Where a company has published several figures for the same thing, this report uses the most recent dated figure and names what it counts.
  • Vendor-sponsored findings are flagged in the text and in the register.
  • Payment records can be a harder measure than surveys, but only for the population they cover. Carta, for example, reports that 57.7% of the fund managers among its U.S. fund administration customers had paid Anthropic or OpenAI in the 12 months to Q3 2026. That describes fund managers’ spending, not GTM teams, so it is not used as evidence here.

2. Adoption has outrun readiness

AI is now standard equipment for revenue teams. Readiness to run it at scale, and evidence that it pays, lag behind.

Figure 1. AI use against readiness, two 2026 vendor surveys

The same pattern appears where outcomes are measured, though most of the measures below are self-assessments:

  • Time saved is not time reinvested. AI saves sellers 4.8 hours a week on average, but most sales organizations report low reinvestment of that time (Figure 5). Organizations with moderate to large time savings that reinvest them in high-impact sales work are 2.2 times as likely to exceed customer-growth goals, and 3.1 times as likely to exceed lead-to-opportunity conversion goals, as those that reinvest less. This is an association among 210 surveyed sales leaders, not a measured effect.
  • More agents, little felt productivity. Gartner predicts agents will outnumber sellers 10 to 1 by 2028, while fewer than 40% of sellers will say agents improved their productivity. Its analyst warns that if the underlying systems are fragmented, “the agents will scale the fragmentation.”
  • Few report revenue impact. In Highspot’s 2025 survey of 463 sales and revenue leaders, 28% said AI improves revenue-driving sales performance. Among 2,002 CIOs and technology executives surveyed by Gartner in 2026, 13% report significant or transformational value from AI.
  • Seller productivity has plateaued. In Gong’s survey of 3,048 revenue leaders, leaders estimated that 46% of their reps reached quota in 2025, down from an estimated 52% in 2024. Gong’s separate analysis of 7.1 million opportunities at 3,613 organizations found win rates and deal length steady in 2025 while reps worked fewer opportunities.

Access is no longer the constraint. The distance between using AI and showing results is a gap in operating model and in measurement, and the rest of this report examines who has narrowed it and how.

3. Function by function: what AI changes

AI’s effects differ by function. Support has the most mature evidence and sales development the most visible change. Customer success has the least public evidence, so its row says so, and section 8 lists tests to run instead. Table 1 sets the reported gains against the costs.

Two patterns cut across the table. The reported gains come first in high-volume, rules-heavy work: inbound qualification, tier-one support, research and data hygiene. And in every function the scarce skill shifts from doing the task to designing, checking and improving the system that does it.

4. Case studies: how the leaders rebuilt the work

Five cases show what the strongest reported results took and what they cost. They were chosen because each company published a figure for a named workflow, with enough detail to say what it counts. They are not a sample: two reached this report as leads from the field, and companies with nothing to show rarely publish. Figure 2 lists their headline rates, each dated and labeled with what it counts. None is an audited figure.

Case 1. Fiserv: unit economics in a regulated call center

  • What changed: Two AI-enabled workflows in Fiserv’s turnaround: an agentic call center built with Sierra, and agents embedded in the risk-hold process at Clover, its merchant platform.
  • Call center (Q3 2026 call, November 3, 2026): A containment rate above 40% and a 5–10x return on token costs. Management said there was no negative effect on customer NPS. It gave no count of eligible contacts and no NPS sample.
  • Clover risk holds (same call): Decision times fell by two-thirds and false positives by more than 40% after agents were embedded. Management gave no period and no count of cases.
  • Company-wide target and costs, not measured AI results: Project Elevate’s savings target rose to $1 billion from $500 million. On the call, management attributed the increase to a portfolio review and to early results from deploying AI; the release names only the review and added efficiencies. The newly identified additional savings will come largely after 2027. Separately, Fiserv excluded $158 million in Q3 and $487 million over 9 months of One Fiserv transformation program expenses from adjusted results. Management linked the two, expecting at least a 1:1 return on Elevate savings against transformation expense (call transcript), but the release does not break the costs down by program.
  • Apply it: Report AI returns per workflow and say what the cost base includes. A return on token costs leaves out build, review, escalation and rework.

Case 2. Salesforce: customer zero, with redeployment

  • What changed: Salesforce runs its own agents on its help site and uses an SDR agent to work low-score leads its people could not reach. Its CEO cited a backlog of 100 million uncalled leads built up over 26 years (TechRadar, September 2, 2025).
  • Results, as Salesforce reports them: Its help agent has passed 5 million customer conversations, with 64% resolved autonomously (earnings call, August 26, 2026; period not stated). Its earlier figures were worded differently each time: a 77% resolution rate in September 2025, 63% of questions resolved on 2.6 million help-site conversations in a year (January 2026, with satisfaction roughly on par with human agents) and 70% of 4.3 million inquiries (June 25, 2026). The four may not be one measure. The SDR agent created 3,200 opportunities in 4 months (early 2026).
  • Staffing, from two sources a few months apart: The CEO said in an interview reported on September 1, 2025 that support headcount had gone from about 9,000 to about 5,000. A company article of January 15, 2026 says the support team shrank through attrition and redeployment and gives no headcount. It also says that hundreds of employees moved into high-growth areas, that the Evaluations team doubled by recruiting from support and that the company is adding thousands of sales and professional services roles.
  • New roles: forward-deployed engineers, deployment strategists, AI conversation designers and AI architects.
  • Caveats: Company figures, not independently verified, from the vendor of the product. Salesforce’s fiscal Q3 results arrive after this report’s cutoff.
  • Apply it: Decide where freed capacity goes before launch, and staff the roles that keep agents good: evaluation, conversation design and deployment.

Case 3. Klarna: two accounts of one decision

  • The 2024 forecast: In February 2024 Klarna said its AI assistant had handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, two-thirds of customer service chats and the work of 700 full-time agents. It estimated a $40 million profit improvement for 2024.
  • The reported outcome for 2024: In a July 2025 letter to SEC staff, Klarna said the assistant delivered about $39 million of cost savings in 2024 and handled 66% of chats in the 12 months to March 31, 2025. AI-handled chats were resolved in about 2 minutes, against a 12-minute average for human agents.
  • The 2025 figures: In its annual report for 2025, Klarna says the assistant handled 80% of customer service chats in the year and saved about $59 million. It puts the assistant’s work at more than 850 full-time agents and says customer satisfaction was on a par with human agents, by its own surveys.
  • The disputed 2025 change of course: In May 2025 the CEO told Bloomberg that cost had weighed too heavily and quality had suffered, and Klarna began recruiting human agents. In its SEC letter, Klarna said the CEO’s quality remarks concerned a pilot of freelance customer experience consultants, not AI service quality, and described a dual track of AI plus high-quality human support. The letter answers a Forbes article and does not name the outlet that ran the interview.
  • Apply it: On either reading the lesson holds: set quality and customer measures beside cost from day one, and keep a route to a person.

Case 4. Vercel: a vendor’s account of building from the best performer

  • Read it as a claim: Vercel sells the platform its agents run on. The figures below come from its own posts, an investor’s write-up of an interview and coverage of a talk. None publishes a denominator, and the figures vary between retellings.
  • What changed: A GTM engineering team builds agents for go-to-market functions. One engineer built the inbound lead agent while spending about a fifth of their time on it, and the top SDR wrote its first instructions (write-up of October 6, 2026).
  • How: The top performer reviewed every output at first, and review later moved to a random sample. When the lead agent’s instructions grew to about 1,000 lines, deterministic rules moved into code and the model kept the judgment calls (same write-up).
  • What Vercel reports, snapshot by snapshot: February 9, 2026: one SDR does the work of 10, and the support agent answers 87% of initial questions. June 17, 2026: the lead agent costs about $5,000 a year to run and returns 32 times that, with an engineer’s part-time work described separately; the support agent solves 92% of tickets; more than 100 agents are in production. October 6, 2026, in the investor’s write-up: about $1,000 a year in inference and infrastructure for the lead agent, plus a fifth of one engineer’s time. October 15, 2026: the support agent automates 91% of support tickets. A later talk, as SaaStr reports it: 93% of total case volume, and a lead agent costing under $5,000 a year in infrastructure and tokens. Whether the 32 times counts the engineer’s time is not stated.
  • Apply it: Start with a workflow your best person can describe step by step, keep that person reviewing until the corrections stop and publish your own denominator.

Case 5. Fin and HubSpot: what a resolution rate measures

  • Fin was called Intercom until May 12, 2026, when the company took the name of its AI agent; the customer service platform kept the Intercom name. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Fin on September 10, 2026, so Fin’s figures are now those of a Salesforce product. The company made itself its own reference customer: it moved its support team to an AI-first model, created a conversation designer role and reports that Fin resolves more than 81% of its own support volume (March 13, 2026). Across customers it reports a 76% average resolution rate, public by June 9, 2026. Fin then narrowed the denominator: conversations in which it could not answer no longer count, for new workspaces from June 25 and for existing ones from July 1 to 8, 2026. That can raise a reported rate with no change in outcomes, and the same 76% is still quoted after the change. Its $0.99 fee applies to confirmed resolutions and to procedure handoffs. It also applies to “assumed” resolutions, where a customer leaves without asking for more help. A clarifying question that gets no reply is not billed, and a resolution is deducted if the customer comes back.
  • HubSpot gives an average resolution rate for Customer Agent on its earnings calls: 55% in August 2025, in the 60s in November 2025, the mid-60s in February 2026, 70% in May 2026 and 72% of support tickets without human escalation in August 2026. In May 2026 it also said the rate had gone “from 20% last year”, with no date for the 20%. In November 2026 it gave no rate and said the agent resolved more than 2 million support issues in the quarter. HubSpot does not say which customers or tickets the rate covers. Separately, it said more than 10,000 customers had adopted Customer Agent by Q2 2026. Its CEO says customers start with internal-facing agents, such as its Data Agent.
  • Apply it: Before comparing vendors or tracking progress, fix one cohort and one definition, sample assumed resolutions, and pay for verified completions where you can.

5. The negative impacts, and who bears them

The costs are real, and they fall unevenly: on customers when quality slips, on early-career workers when entry-level work is automated and on teams asked to run new tools on old processes.

What happens to the people

Figure 3. Workforce actions reported by customer service leaders

More service leaders report moving agents into other roles than cutting headcount. Gartner’s release ties only the headcount cut to AI, and it does not say whether respondents could report several actions. Few revenue leaders expect replacement: in Apollo’s 2026 survey of 328 GTM professionals, a vendor survey, 6% of sales and marketing leaders believe AI will replace members of their team. Gartner advises treating headcount reductions as the result of proven, sustained AI performance rather than a precondition for value.

The pressure lands hardest at the entry level. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab finds that employment of U.S. workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations, customer service among them, is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed occupations. That is a relative gap in payroll data, not a count of jobs lost. The lab finds no economy-wide displacement, and the decline is concentrated where AI automates work rather than complements it.

Ten costs to plan for

Table 2. The main negative impacts, the evidence and how leaders mitigate them

Negative impact Evidence Who bears it How leaders mitigate it
Quality and trust erode when cost leads Klarna’s disputed 2025 change of course (Case 3); 87% of customers say companies using GenAI must offer a route to a human, and only 27% would try a chatbot again after a bad experience (Gartner, 3,566 customers) Customers and the brand Hold quality measures beside cost; keep a visible route to a person
Cut fast, rehire later Gartner predicts half of the companies that cut service staff because of AI will rehire by 2027; some already have (Figure 3) Workers and the cost base Reduce headcount only after AI performance is proven and sustained
A narrower entry-level ladder Stanford’s 19% relative employment gap for U.S. workers aged 22 to 25 in highly exposed occupations Early-career workers and tomorrow’s managers Rebuild entry roles around reviewing, correcting and supervising AI work
Outbound saturation risk Instantly reports a 3.43% average reply rate, counting all replies over all emails sent, and describes reply rates as stable while volume grows; no source here isolates the effect of AI-written email Domain reputation, the brand and prospects Track positive replies or qualified meetings per eligible account; cap volume; review new messaging
Saved time leaks away AI saves sellers 4.8 hours a week, and most sales organizations report low reinvestment of it (Figure 5) Sellers and the productivity case Name where each recovered hour goes before launch
Agent and tool sprawl Gartner forecasts agents outnumbering sellers 10 to 1 by 2028, with fewer than 40% of sellers saying agents helped; poor integration keeps teams from fully using current platforms (Figure 5) Sellers’ attention and RevOps One shared context layer; retire tools when agents replace them
Data and process debt exposed Poor data quality and undocumented processes rank high among the reasons AI underperforms (Figure 5); data and analytics leaders estimate that 19% of their company’s data is siloed, inaccessible or otherwise unusable (Salesforce) RevOps and forecast accuracy Fix data and document processes before automating them
Buyers route around reps 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience and 70% a completely digital, self-service one (Gartner) AEs’ influence early in the cycle Make content AI-readable; position reps as the people who validate what AI told the buyer
A governance gap 5% of companies have all six of BCG’s controls for agents in place, though 42% expect to give agents decision-making authority by 2030 (BCG) Risk, legal and customers An owner, evaluations, cost caps and rollback for every agent
Pressure on middle management Companies expect workforce reductions of 10–15% by 2030, with middle management and frontline leadership the most exposed layers (BCG; a forecast) Front-line and middle managers Redefine managers as coaches and supervisors of mixed human-agent teams

6. What leaders do differently

Across independent studies, the companies reporting results share an operating model, not a tool list. The studies compare groups, and several define the groups by the outcome itself, so read the gaps as associations and test the practices in your own data.

Figure 4. Market-share leaders against laggards in B2B

McKinsey grouped companies by change in market share: leaders grew share by more than 10% in a year, and laggards lost more than 5%. Other studies point the same way, with the same limits:

  • BCG finds that the 7.5% of companies it calls future-built had 2.4 times the revenue growth, 2.3 times the shareholder return and 2.8 times the EBITDA growth of laggards over 2022 to 2025, figures it takes from financial databases, and that a further 41% are scaling AI and also outperforming. Its groups are defined by AI maturity. In its 2025 study, future-built companies had deployed 62% of their AI initiatives, against 12% for laggards.
  • Bain’s “winners,” selected for top-quartile revenue growth in their sector and region and for beating margin targets, report twice the AI-attributed revenue growth of laggards. Bain presents their redesign of work as a description of how they operate; it does not test cause.
  • Gong, a vendor, finds in its platform records that sellers who use AI frequently generate 77% more revenue per rep than those who do not, across 7.1 million opportunities at 3,613 organizations. It also reports that organizations with AI at the core of their strategy are 65% more likely to have raised win rates than those running limited pilots, and does not say which data that figure rests on.
  • Gartner finds that sales organizations giving sellers AI next-best actions are 2.6 times as likely to achieve commercial growth, and that those prioritizing upskilling sellers on AI are 2.4 times as likely to report strong revenue growth. Its release ties a survey of 227 CSOs, fielded August to September 2025, to the upskilling figure and names no sample for the first.

None of these proves that AI caused the difference; better-run companies may simply adopt AI faster. The practices behind the gaps are consistent, though, and each can be tested.

Table 3. Eight practices associated with leaders, and how to test them

Practice What it looks like Evidence (associations unless noted) How to test it
1. Redesign the workflow before automating it Map the work end to end, codify the best performer, then decide what agents do Bain’s top performers describe redesigning work; BCG’s future-built companies redesign workflows end to end; in a causal field study at one company, less experienced support agents gained most from AI assistance (QJE); one vendor account (Case 4) Compare a redesigned workflow with an automate-as-is version on the same unit of work
2. Concentrate on a few high-volume workflows A short list, each with a measurable unit and a single owner BCG’s future-built companies set priorities for where AI creates value Track value per workflow, not per program
3. Measure per unit of work, against a comparison group Fully loaded cost per verified completion; quality against a human baseline BCG’s leaders measure impact in the P&L. Separately, organizations with rules for stopping weak pilots are 2.3 times as likely to be in Gartner’s top-performing group Use the measurement protocol in section 8
4. Keep people on judgment, exceptions and money Full review until a predeclared quality margin holds, then sampling; a clear route to a person Buyers are 39 points more likely to say a rep, rather than GenAI, understood their needs (Gartner) Report review coverage and override rates separately
5. Reinvest freed capacity on purpose Decide in advance where hours and roles go Gartner’s reinvestment finding (section 2); Salesforce moved support capacity toward sales Record hours released, hours redeployed and cash savings separately
6. Build capability inside the team GTM engineers, evaluation teams, conversation designers Salesforce doubled its Evaluations team; Fin created a conversation designer role; GTM engineering and RevOps postings, counted together, up 205% in January to September 2025 against the same months of 2024 (Bloomberry) Time from idea to production agent; share of agents with an owner and evaluations
7. Make AI fluency a job requirement Hiring bars, performance reviews and headcount requests that assume AI Shopify asks teams to show why AI cannot do the work before asking for more headcount and resources; Zapier requires AI fluency of every new hire; upskilling sellers on AI is associated with strong revenue growth (Gartner) Fluency levels by role, tracked against unit-of-work results
8. Govern agents like a workforce A named owner, evaluations, cost caps, rollback and a plan for human-agent roles Organizations with explicit plans to redesign roles for people and agents are 2.4 times as likely to be in Gartner’s top-performing group, yet 4% of CIOs report such plans (Gartner) Controls coverage across agents (section 9)

Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index describes the same shift from the employee’s side. As agent use grows, human involvement changes shape rather than disappearing, and its most advanced users are more likely than others to document agent workflows, handoffs and quality standards so that colleagues can repeat them.

7. What holds the laggards back

The barriers leaders name are mostly operational. Few surveys find the models themselves to be the binding constraint; most point to what surrounds them.

Figure 5. Barriers leaders name, survey by survey

Seven patterns recur in the laggards’ record:

  1. Tools layered on unchanged workflows. Gartner warns that agents placed on fragmented systems multiply the fragmentation, and predicts that by 2028 chief sales officers who overhaul data, automation and user experience will be 5 times as likely to gain a return on AI as those who choose quick fixes.
  2. Data and process debt. Bad data, undocumented processes and siloed teams are the root causes GTM practitioners named in LeanData’s survey when AI underperforms. Agents inherit every gap in the CRM and every step nobody wrote down.
  3. No plan for freed capacity. Without a reinvestment plan, saved hours are absorbed by lower-value work, and the productivity case never reaches the P&L.
  4. Measuring activity instead of outcomes. Only 31% of CIOs have rules for stopping an AI pilot before production, and 17% have rules for retiring low-value AI that is already running (Gartner).
  5. Cost as the only objective. Klarna’s experience, on either reading (Case 3), and Gartner’s warning against cutting fast and rehiring later show the risk when savings lead and quality follows.
  6. Missing controls. In BCG’s survey, 5% of companies have all six of its controls for agents in place (Table 2).
  7. Unchanged roles, skills and incentives. Only 4% of CIOs report explicit plans to redesign roles for a human-agent workforce (Gartner), and even among knowledge workers who already use AI, Microsoft classes just 16% as Frontier Professionals, its most advanced users.

8. A 90-day playbook

The leaders’ sequence can be compressed into one quarter for a first set of workflows. Each phase ends at a gate, and the next phase starts only when the gate is passed. Day 90 supports a decision to scale, hold or stop a workflow. A hold is a valid result: it means the evidence is not in yet. Outcomes that take longer to show, such as renewals, need a longer observation window.

Figure 6. A 90-day path from chosen workflow to a scale decision

Table 4. Measurement protocol for each workflow

Element What to record Why it matters
Cost basis Total cost of all assigned cases, including agent run costs, implementation, review, escalation and rework, divided by verified completions; the same accounting for the comparison group A vendor fee or a return on token costs is not a fully loaded cost
Volume funnel Eligible, attempted, handed-off and verified-complete counts, every week A narrower denominator can raise a reported rate with no change in outcomes
Quality Satisfaction, accuracy or conversion against the human baseline, plus a separate sample of silent exits and assumed resolutions Silent exits can be counted as success and billed as outcomes
Review Review coverage, the share of work a person checks, reported separately from overrides among reviewed cases Fewer reviews can make the override rate look better
Commercial impact Hours released, hours redeployed and cash savings, recorded separately; incremental conversion, gross profit or retention against the comparison group, kept as coverage expands Shows whether freed capacity produced growth
Decision rule Declared before launch: a quality margin against the baseline, critical-error rules, a minimum volume and an observation window Keeps the scale decision from being argued after the fact

Decisions to make in week one

  1. Which workflows. Three to five, each with a unit of work (a lead, a ticket, a renewal) and a single owner.
  2. What counts as success. The cost basis, quality margin and comparison group in Table 4, set before launch rather than read from before-and-after anecdotes.
  3. Where freed capacity goes. Named in advance: outbound, expansion, strategic accounts or slower backfill.
  4. Who builds. A GTM engineer or builder, paired with the function’s best performer.
  5. What would stop an agent. Critical-error rules, cost caps and a rollback path, agreed before launch.

Tests to run in customer success. Public evidence is thin here, so run these in your own data: whether agent-flagged renewal risk shows up earlier than your team’s own signals; whether value reviews can be prepared faster with no loss of accuracy; whether digital-only coverage loses relationship signal.

9. A metrics scorecard

Leaders measure AI by the unit of work, not by adoption. Table 5 lists the measures to track and, where one exists, a public reference point with its limits. Treat the reference points as orientation, not targets: each comes from a different company, measured its own way, and most are self-reported.

Table 5. Scorecard for AI in go-to-market

Metric What it measures Why it matters Public reference points and their limits
Fully loaded cost per verified completion Total cost of assigned cases, including implementation, review, escalation and rework, divided by verified completions Decides whether to build, buy or redeploy No public example meets this standard. Fin’s $0.99 fee also applies to assumed resolutions and procedure handoffs; Fiserv’s 5–10x return counts token costs only
Verified completion rate Verified completions over eligible units, shown with the eligible, attempted and handed-off counts Separates real automation from a narrower denominator Published rates (Figure 2) use different denominators, and Fin narrowed its own in June and July 2026
Quality against the baseline Satisfaction, accuracy or conversion against the human baseline on the same work Shows cost is not being traded for quality Salesforce and Klarna each report satisfaction on a par with human agents, by their own measures
Silent-exit sample Share of silent exits and assumed resolutions that were actually resolved, from a separate sample Catches false resolutions Fin counts a customer leaving without asking for more help, or 24 hours of inactivity, as a resolution, and deducts it if the customer comes back
Speed to lead and to resolution Minutes from signal to first response, and from contact to resolution Often the first and cleanest gain Klarna: about 2 minutes for AI-handled chats against a 12-minute human average in 2024
Repeat-contact rate Share of issues that come back A second check on false resolutions Klarna reported 25% fewer repeat inquiries
Hours released, redeployed and saved Three separate figures: hours freed, hours moved to planned work, cash saved Where most of the value leaks 72% of sales organizations report low reinvestment (Gartner)
Incremental commercial impact Conversion, gross profit or retention against the comparison group Shows whether redeployment produced growth Gong’s platform records show 77% more revenue per rep for sellers who frequently use AI (vendor; correlational)
Positive replies or qualified meetings per eligible account Outbound results per account in scope, not per email sent Avoids rewarding volume Instantly’s 3.43% average counts all replies over all emails sent
Review coverage and override rate Share of agent work reviewed, and share of reviewed work corrected, reported separately The gate for stepping review down No public example reports both figures; one vendor account describes moving from full review to sampling (Case 4)
AI fluency coverage Share of staff at a defined fluency level A leading indicator of how deep adoption runs Zapier assesses every hire against a four-level fluency rubric
Controls coverage Share of agents with an owner, evaluations, cost caps and rollback Governance before scale BCG counts something different: 5% of companies have all six of its controls for agents in place across the enterprise

10. Outlook: November 2026 to November 2028

Five shifts look likely over the next 24 months, each grounded in a forecast or a trend already under way. Forecasts for 2030 fall outside this window and are listed separately below.

  1. Agents multiply, and our read is that value moves to orchestration. Gartner expects agents to outnumber sellers 10 to 1 by 2028, while fewer than 40% of sellers say agents improved their productivity. On that forecast the constraint becomes coordination, data and governance, not access to agents. This is a read and no study has tested it, and two early experiments cut against it. In a randomized trial on 100 websites, a single sales agent raised revenue per visitor by 10.0%. In a controlled comparison across 13 enterprise-style procedures, coordinated agent designs used 1.4 to 4.7 times the tokens of a single agent with no overall gain in success. Both are preprints that have not been peer reviewed, and neither tests live GTM work across a revenue process.
  2. Buyers arrive briefed by AI. 45% of B2B buyers already report using GenAI in a recent purchase, and 69% prefer to validate AI-generated insights with a sales rep (Gartner). McKinsey finds gen AI now ranks among the top five channels buyers use to find and evaluate suppliers. Sellers’ value shifts toward validation, quantification and confidence. On the seller side, Gartner predicts that 95% of sellers’ research workflows will begin with AI by 2027.
  3. Service stays hybrid. Gartner predicts none of the Fortune 500 will have fully eliminated human customer service by 2028. Expect fewer, more skilled people working the complex cases.
  4. Entry-level roles get redesigned. Stanford’s lab now updates its young-worker measures monthly, so the 19% gap will show whether entry-level pressure is spreading. GTM engineering is the first revenue role built around agent work, and entry roles will need redesigning around reviewing and supervising AI.
  5. Pricing follows the work. Per-resolution and usage pricing are spreading, led by Fin and Salesforce, which now owns it. Revenue teams will increasingly sell, forecast and renew in units of work done, and the definition of a billable outcome becomes a negotiating point.

Longer-range forecasts, outside this window. BCG projects that agentic AI will account for about 40% of AI value by 2030, up from 22% in 2026 and 17% in 2025, and that dedicated AI roles will grow from 7% of the workforce in 2026 to 22% by 2030. Companies in its survey expect workforce reductions of 10–15% by 2030, with middle management and frontline leadership the most exposed layers. These are forecasts, not observations.

Five questions for the next leadership offsite

  1. Which three workflows would we rebuild first, and who owns each?
  2. What does a verified unit of work cost us today, by person and by agent?
  3. Where will freed capacity go, and how will we know it got there?
  4. How will new sellers and CSMs learn the craft if AI does the entry-level work?
  5. What result, declared in advance, would make us scale, hold or stop an agent?

Appendix A: Evidence register

Each finding as used in this report. The grade (section 1) says what kind of evidence a finding is, and the basis says how it was produced. Neither says whether a figure has been independently verified. A forecast or a target is graded C whatever its units. Two rows are context and one is a methods example, and none of the three is used as evidence.

The register has its own page on this site, where every finding can be searched and filtered and links to its source. Open the evidence register.

Appendix B: Sources and caveats

Caveats. Check these before reusing any figure.

  • Coverage. Evidence runs through November 23, 2026. The narrative in sections 1 to 10 is the edition of November 20, 2026. Records added since are in Appendix A. The Q3 2026 earnings season is incomplete, and companies with off-calendar quarters, including Salesforce, report after the cutoff.
  • Who compiled and reviewed it. Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, compiled the findings and checked each against the source it links to. Nathan Fierley edited the report and decided what went in. On November 20, 2026 a second AI model, GPT-6.2 Astra, made by OpenAI, rechecked the 54 findings then in the register and disputed 23. Of those, 22 were confirmed and corrected that day, and the last, Carta’s, on November 24, 2026, once a person had opened its page. Later that day 11 records were added: five from ICONIQ, four from Deloitte, one from Citi and one from HubSpot. The Fiserv row on Project Elevate was also corrected a second time, after a reader pointed to the reasons management gave. None of these was part of that recheck. On November 22, 2026, 12 more records were added and three rows corrected, each after two source checks by Claude and outside that recheck. Five of the 12 are from BCG and two are on SAP, and those seven reached the register as leads from the field. The other five are from earnings calls. The three corrections replace or date figures from Salesforce and HubSpot. On November 23, 2026, eight more records were added, each after two source checks by Claude and outside that recheck. Six came from a weekly scan of new publications and two from a lookback over 18 months of earnings calls. The same day a model from another lab checked the eight against their sources. It disputed no figure. Five rows were reworded and three links were replaced with the publishers’ own releases, as Appendix C lists. On November 25, 2026, five more records were added, each after two source checks by Claude and outside that recheck. All five reached the register as leads from the field: one from Monaco and four from Anthropic. The report has not been peer reviewed, and no outside expert has reviewed it.
  • Vendor sources. Many sources are vendors reporting on their own products, their customers or their own platform’s data: Vercel, Salesforce, Fin (part of Salesforce since September 10, 2026), HubSpot, ServiceNow, Microsoft, Gong, LeanData, Salesloft, Instantly, Seismic, Highspot, Apollo, Bloomberry, ChurnZero, Richardson, SnapLogic, Zendesk, Monaco and Anthropic. Read their figures as claims.
  • Definitions. Resolution, containment, handling and automation are defined differently by each company, and Fin narrowed its resolution-rate denominator between June 25 and July 8, 2026. The rates in Figure 2 are not like-for-like.
  • Associations. Leader-versus-laggard comparisons (McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Gong, Gartner) compare groups at one point in time, and several define the groups by outcome. They do not show that AI caused the difference.
  • Causal evidence. The QJE field study is causal for support agents at one company; it does not automatically carry over to other functions. Two arXiv preprints report experiments: a randomized trial of one sales agent on websites, and a controlled comparison of agent designs on enterprise-style procedures. Neither has been peer reviewed, and neither tests live GTM work across a revenue process.
  • Vercel. Figures come from the company’s posts, an investor’s write-up of an interview and coverage of a talk, without published denominators, and they vary between retellings. Case 4 lists each dated figure with what it counts.
  • Klarna. The 2024 profit figure was a forecast. The reported 2024 savings come from Klarna’s letter to SEC staff, and the 2025 figures from its annual report. The 2025 change of course has two accounts (Case 3).
  • Fiserv. Call-center results, Clover risk-hold results, Project Elevate savings and One Fiserv transformation expenses have different scopes and are kept separate. The release gives a portfolio review as the reason for the higher Elevate target, and the call adds early results from deploying AI. One transcript marks the word before “rate above 40%” as inaudible, and a second reads “a containment rate above 40%”.
  • BCG. The full report says its financial multiples come from Capital IQ and Orbis for 2022 to 2025. It was read in a copy hosted on another site. BCG’s 2025 edition, on BCG’s own site, says the same of its figures.
  • Gartner. Four releases, dated May 11, July 28, September 2 and October 19, 2026, would not open for the checker and were read through search results that show their text.
  • Deloitte. The survey covers only companies that already have AI in daily use, so its shares are not shares of all companies. Its multi-agent figures rest on the 2,372 companies that run several agents in one workflow. Deloitte advises companies on AI.
  • Citi. The figure counts Citi’s own engineers, not GTM staff, and the call does not give their total. It is in the register as an adoption figure from the earnings record.
  • ICONIQ. An investor’s survey of executives at software companies that build AI products, some of them its own portfolio companies. Its shares describe that group and not companies in general. Several of its figures are executives’ estimates, and the shares for headcount plans are sums of the bands the report prints.
  • BCG’s survey of revenue leaders. A survey of 398 revenue leaders, published October 19, 2026, with no fieldwork dates. Its chart labels the impact figures as the share ranking each area first or second, while its text words them as shares that report an improvement. The gaps it reports for organizations with more autonomous agents are associations, and it gives no threshold or size for that group.
  • SAP. The figures come from an article in HBR by two Harvard Business School authors (March 27, 2025), which does not say how the authors obtained them. No SAP document was opened. The shorter sales cycle compares the Digital Hubs with SAP’s in-person selling to large customers, so it is not a like-for-like test of AI.
  • Earnings calls in third-party transcripts. The rows added or corrected on November 22, 2026 from Salesforce, HubSpot, ServiceNow, FactSet, JPMorgan, HCLTech and Infosys were read in transcripts published by other sites, not in company documents. So were the rows added on November 23, 2026 from Lowe’s and Walmart.
  • Lowe’s and Walmart. Both are consumer retailers, outside B2B selling. Each compares customers who use an AI shopping assistant with customers who do not. Neither call describes an assignment or an adjustment, or gives a sample, a period or a method, so the gap is an association between two groups and not a measured lift.
  • Fin on Salesforce’s help portal. Fin’s page gives no publication date and no count or period for the 62%. Salesforce’s post of November 9, 2026 gives the same 62% for the first few weeks after launch. Neither says how Fin relates to the help agent whose 64% is in Figure 2. Fin’s page says Fin was to handle every conversation on the English-language portal from November 18, and does not say that it has.
  • Microsoft’s internal study. The post gives no number of sellers or deals, no period and no comparison group, and it does not say which product was measured. Its footnote cites internal telemetry from a controlled environment and CRM data.
  • Richardson. Richardson sells sales training. Its two groups are defined by quota attainment, which respondents report themselves, and its release calls the comparisons correlational. The two groups hold 835 of the 1,105 leaders, and the other 270 are in neither. The 70% and the 4% are in the release and not on the report page. The full report sits behind a form and was not opened.
  • SnapLogic. The report does not define an abandoned project or give a period for it. The body of its release says AI projects where the headline and the report say agentic AI projects, and the release gives 64% for moderate or significant overspend where the report’s shares add to 63%. The 89% is of the respondents who answered the question on overspend, and counts slight overspend with moderate and significant.
  • Gartner’s survey on the CMO role. The figures are expectations. The release describes the 282 respondents as senior executive leaders and does not say whether all are C-level, whether CMOs were among them or which countries were covered.
  • Zendesk. Two surveys in 10 countries, one of business respondents and one of consumers, weighted by Zendesk, with no fieldwork firm named. Business leaders are 74% of the business respondents and human agents 26%. Zendesk sells customer service software.
  • Monaco. The figures are the chief executive’s own account, in a podcast interview, of how his company uses the platform it sells. He defines no outbound opportunity and gives no reply, meeting or conversion rate and no baseline. The months are not dated, and the 500 is a pace for a month still under way. He tells customers not to expect the same, because the outreach goes out in his name.
  • Anthropic’s interview study. Anthropic makes Claude, the model that compiled this register. The 58 companies are Anthropic’s own enterprise customers, chosen for range and not as a representative sample. The interview dates are not given and value is as interviewees described it. An automated reviewer, whose model is not named, coded the applications. Three of the four rows are single cases from unnamed companies, with no figures.
  • Forecasts. Gartner’s 2027 and 2028 figures and BCG’s 2030 figures are predictions. Stanford’s findings are descriptive, not causal.
  • Carta. Cited as a methods example only. Its 57.7% covers the management companies of Carta’s U.S.-based fund administration customers, most of them VC firms, and counts payments to Anthropic or OpenAI in the 12 months to Q3 2026. The row was corrected on November 24, 2026, after a second reader reported a narrower population than it gave.

Playbooks

Three plays for the next quarter: enable one agent properly, orchestrate the team around it and reach a decision in 90 days.

Enable an agentOrchestrate the team90 daysWorkshops and guides

Enable an agent the way you onboard a new hire

Every part of a good onboarding program has an agent equivalent. When a pilot stalls, look first for the step that was skipped.

For a new hireFor an agentFrom the evidence
Role and territoryA charter: one unit of work, what is in scope and what it must never doBCG’s future-built companies set priorities for where AI creates value
Onboarding and product knowledgeContext: approved knowledge, account history, CRM fields and permissions70% of GTM practitioners say poor data quality degrades execution (LeanData, a vendor survey)
The top rep’s playbookInstructions written from the best performer’s actual processIn a peer-reviewed field study, less experienced support agents gained most from AI assistance; its authors offer suggestive evidence that the tool spread the practices of more able agents
Ride-alongs and coachingShadow mode: review every output until corrections stop, then sampleOne vendor, Vercel, describes reviewing every output first and sampling later; the report found no study of when to step down
CertificationAn evaluation set of real cases, run before every changeSalesforce doubled its Evaluations team by recruiting from support
Quota and scorecardVerified completions, quality against the human baseline and fully loaded cost per completionFin, now part of Salesforce, narrowed its resolution-rate denominator in June and July 2026, which can raise a reported rate with no change in outcomes
A managerA named owner, an escalation path and a weekly review4% of CIOs report explicit plans to redesign roles for people and agents (Gartner)
Performance managementCost caps, a tested rollback and rules for retiring an agent17% of CIOs have rules for retiring low-value AI that is already running (Gartner)
Write the agent charterRun the launch checklist

Orchestration keeps people and agents working from one record

Gartner expects agents to outnumber sellers 10 to 1 by 2028. Its analyst puts the risk plainly: on fragmented systems, “the agents will scale the fragmentation.”

  1. PeopleOwners, sellers, customer success and reviewers: judgment, exceptions, relationships and money
  2. AgentsOne per unit of work: lead, research, support, renewal preparation
  3. OrchestrationRouting, handoffs, approvals, escalation and a log of every step
  4. Shared contextAccounts, commitments, history and permissions that every agent and person reads from
  5. Systems of recordCRM, billing, support desk and product usage, kept as they are
  • Keep the systems of record.Add only what none of them holds: the shared context and the rules.
  • Stay vendor-neutral.Models and agents will change; your context, rules and measures should not have to.
  • Let every handoff carry the promise.What was committed to the customer travels with the work, so the next agent or person starts from it.
  • Measure the whole workflow.Cost per verified completion from end to end, across every agent and person involved.

A worked handoff: preparing a renewal

An example to adapt, not a finding. The days are example values.

QuestionThe answer, written down before launch
What starts it90 days before the renewal date, the research agent drafts a value readout from product usage, support history and the commitments made at sale
Which record winsThe shared account record. Where it disagrees with the CRM on a commitment, the signed order form decides and the difference is logged
Who acceptsThe customer success manager who owns the account accepts the readout or sends it back with a reason
By whenWithin 2 working days
If nobody doesOn day 3 it goes to the head of customer success, and nothing reaches the customer until a person has accepted it
What it costsThe agent’s run cost, the manager’s review time and any rework all count toward the cost of one verified renewal preparation

Our synthesis, not a finding. Public evidence on orchestration is still thin, two preprints already cut against it and the home page says what would change our read.

Check your maturity

Ninety days to a scale, hold or stop decision

One quarter is enough to decide on a first set of workflows. Each phase ends at a gate, and the next starts only when the evidence passes it. A hold at day 90 is a valid result: it means the evidence is not in yet. Renewals and other slow outcomes need a longer window.

Days 1 to 30: choose and baseline

  • Pick three to five high-volume workflows, each with one owner
  • Write down the best performer’s process
  • Baseline cost and quality on the same unit of work
  • Decide where freed time goes
1Gate 1: baseline set and a comparison group in place

Days 31 to 60: build and shadow

  • Build with the top performer
  • Review every output and log each correction
  • Move fixed rules into code
  • Add cost caps and a rollback
2Gate 2: the predeclared quality margin held over the minimum volume

Days 61 to 90: scale and redeploy

  • Step review down to samples
  • Widen to the whole workflow
  • Redeploy capacity as planned; reset quotas and comp plans
  • Report verified unit costs

Throughout: AI fluency in every role, a GTM engineer, clean and connected data, and an owner and controls for every agent.

Decisions to make in week one

  1. Which workflows. Three to five, each with a unit of work (a lead, a ticket, a renewal) and a single owner.
  2. What counts as success. The cost basis, quality margin and comparison group, set before launch.
  3. Where freed capacity goes. Named in advance: outbound, expansion, strategic accounts or slower backfill.
  4. Who builds. A GTM engineer or builder, paired with the function’s best performer.
  5. What would stop an agent. Critical-error rules, cost caps and a rollback path, agreed before launch.

Measurement protocol

ElementWhat to recordWhy it matters
Cost basisTotal cost of all assigned cases, including run costs, implementation, review, escalation and rework, divided by verified completions; the same for the comparison groupA vendor fee or a return on token costs is not a fully loaded cost
Volume funnelEligible, attempted, handed-off and verified-complete counts, every weekA narrower denominator can raise a rate with no change in outcomes
QualitySatisfaction, accuracy or conversion against the human baseline, plus a separate sample of silent exitsSilent exits can be counted as success and billed as outcomes
ReviewReview coverage, reported separately from overrides among reviewed casesFewer reviews can make the override rate look better
Commercial impactHours released, hours redeployed and cash saved, kept apart; incremental conversion or retention against the comparison groupShows whether freed capacity produced growth
Decision ruleDeclared before launch: quality margin, critical-error rules, minimum volume, observation windowKeeps the scale decision from being argued after the fact

Scorecard, with public reference points and their limits

MetricWhat it measuresReference point and its limits
Fully loaded cost per verified completionTotal cost of assigned cases divided by verified completionsNo public example meets the standard yet. Fin’s $0.99 fee also covers assumed resolutions and procedure handoffs, and Fiserv’s 5–10x return counts token costs only
Verified completion rateVerified completions over eligible units, shown with the funnel countsPublished rates use different denominators, and Fin narrowed its own in June and July 2026
Quality against the baselineSatisfaction, accuracy or conversion against people doing the same workSalesforce and Klarna each report satisfaction on a par with human agents, by their own measures

Workshops and guides

AI-fluency audit for GTM teams

A 3-hour facilitated workshop for 8 to 12 people from sales, marketing and customer success. The team sorts its recurring work three ways (an agent, an on-demand specialist or an accountable person), reads its level off a four-level maturity model and leaves with an action plan.

The facilitator kit is not public. It is shared with teams that run the workshop.

Configuring the Claude Sales plugin

An interactive guide to setting the plugin up for a company, and how the configuration differs for SDRs, account executives and account managers.

Why it is listed: Nathan Fierley wrote it. Claude is made by Anthropic, whose model also compiles this site’s findings. No one pays to be listed here.

Open the guide

Tools

Four working tools for the plays. Each opens with example values; what you enter stays in this browser.

Unit costAgent charterLaunch checklistMaturity check

Unit cost: the fully loaded cost of a verified completion

Example values for a support workflow, per month. They are an illustration, not data.

Fully loaded cost per verified completion

Assumes every case is completed in the end, that closures failing verification are redone by a person and that review time is charged at the reviewer rate.

With the agent$4.93
People only$7.50

34% lower modeled cost with the agent: $25,680 a month. It becomes cash only if the freed capacity is redeployed or removed.

  • Agent run cost$6,500
  • Implementation$4,000
  • Review$5,400
  • People, on cases the agent did not close$27,750
  • Rework, on closures that failed verification$5,670

Why headline numbers differ

  • 7.3xreturn on reported closures, run cost alone, as a headline would count it
  • 6.4xreturn on verified closures, run cost alone
  • 2.6xreturn on verified closures, fully loaded
  • 63%closed by the agent, as reported
  • 55%of assigned cases verified complete by the agent

Return is handling cost avoided, divided by what the agent costs. Published returns can count run cost only: Fiserv’s 5–10x is a return on token costs.

Agent charter

One page per agent. The example is an inbound lead agent; edit any field and copy the result.

Your charter

Agent: Inbound lead agent
Unit of work: One inbound demo request
Owner: Head of sales development
Approver: Chief revenue officer, for any change to scope, permissions or the cost cap
Freed capacity goes to: Outbound to target accounts
In scope: Research the company and contact, sort the lead into four routes (book a meeting, pass to a seller, nurture or decline), draft the reply
Out of scope: Pricing, discounts, contract terms
Never: Send without review during shadow mode; contact an account with an open support escalation
Context: CRM account and contact records, product usage, approved messaging, routing rules
Permissions: Read the CRM, write drafts and notes; no send rights until gate 2
Escalate to a person when: The account is a named account or in an open opportunity, or the request is unclear
Evaluation set: 200 past requests with the route and reply the top SDR chose
Quality margin: Meetings per eligible lead within 2 points of the human baseline
Review: Every output until 2 weeks pass without a correction, then a 10% sample
Cost cap: $600 a month in run costs, with an alert at $480
Decision rule: Scale if the margin holds over 4 weeks and 1,000 leads. If the volume is short at day 90, hold and keep measuring. If the margin fails, stop

Five items are ticked as an example. Untick them to start your own. The ticks are your own report, and nothing checks them.

Maturity check

Pick the cell that best describes your team in each row; example answers are filled in. The four levels are the ones the AI-fluency audit uses, and the same rule applies: your weakest dimension sets your level. Level 4 reflects our read that teams are heading toward orchestration, which no public study has tested yet.

Level 1: Manual

You are at level 1 because handoffs and governance and roles are your lowest dimensions.

Next moves.Handoffs: Write down who receives each agent’s output and when a person steps in.Governance and roles: Name an owner for every agent in production.

Evidence

The findings behind the GTM report, each with its population, period, basis, grade and source. Evidence runs through November 23, 2026.

The register

Of the 99 records in the register, 76 are self-reported, 12 are observed in records, 7 are forecasts and 4 are estimates. Three are context rows or a methods example and are not used as evidence. Two are causal studies, one of them a preprint. Each square is one record, marked with its grade.

CCCC

Grade says what a finding can prove: A, stated in financial terms; B, a measured result; C, a survey, forecast or narrative. A forecast or a target is C whatever its units. Basis says how it was produced. Neither means a figure was independently verified. Records are listed by grade, then by basis, with vendor sources last.

Unless a row says otherwise, Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, spotted and compiled the finding and checked it against the source the row links to. Nathan Fierley edited it. A row marked “Spotted by” came from a person in the field or from an outside review.

On November 20, 2026 a second AI model, GPT-6.2 Astra, made by OpenAI, rechecked the 54 findings then in the register against their sources and disputed 23. Of those, 22 were confirmed and corrected. Two of them were split in two and four more rows were regraded or reworded at the same time, so 28 rows were corrected that day. One disputed row waits for a person to open its source. Since that recheck 23 records have been added and three rows corrected, each after source checks by Claude. None of them carries the recheck.

About Modern GTM

An evidence-led library on running go-to-market teams of people and agents.

What this is for

Of the 99 records collected here, 76 are self-reported: a company or a survey respondent describing its own results. Modern GTM grades each finding by what it can prove and turns what holds up into plays and tools a team can run next quarter.

Our read is that agent enablement and orchestration are the next horizon for GTM teams. As agents multiply, results will depend less on access to AI and more on how well each agent is prepared and how well people and agents are coordinated. No public study has tested this yet, and the home page says what would change that read.

Modern GTM is curated by Nathan Fierley, who is also building Zeal, an early-stage project on shared GTM context for people and agents, a subject this site covers. Zeal is not cited as evidence here.

Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, compiles each finding and checks it against the source its row links to. Nathan Fierley decides what goes in and edits what is published. A second AI model, GPT-6.2 Astra, made by OpenAI, rechecked the register on November 20, 2026. Nothing here has been peer reviewed, and no outside expert has reviewed it.

No one pays to appear on this site. Vendors and AI labs, Anthropic and OpenAI among them, can send findings the same way as anyone else, and their figures are checked, graded and marked as vendor sources.

Privacy. Cloudflare serves this site. It counts visits with its Web Analytics, which sets no cookies and stores nothing in your browser, and it reports which AI crawlers visit. Nothing on the site identifies a visitor: it carries no tracking pixels, advertising tags or marketing scripts. A proposal filed on GitHub is public there, under GitHub’s terms.

Findings and corrections are welcome from people and from AI agents acting for them. How to contribute.

How the evidence is graded

  • A FinancialThe effect is stated in financial terms, such as a cost saving, a return or a profit improvement, and it has been reported, not forecast.
  • B MeasuredA quantified operating or labor-market result, with no financial translation.
  • C Survey, forecast or narrativePerceptions, predictions, comparisons between groups or qualitative claims.

Basis. Each finding is also marked as observed in records or accounts, self-reported by a company or respondent, estimated, or forecast.

Rules. One dated figure per claim, with what it counts. A forecast or a target is graded C whatever its units. Leader-versus-laggard gaps are labeled as associations. A vendor is a source that sells the product it measures, reports from its own platform’s data or surveys the market it sells to, and vendors are flagged. A company reporting on its own operations is not a vendor. Example values in the tools are marked as examples.

A weekly scan of earnings material, new research, industry news and published customer stories runs each Monday. It files proposals, and a person approves each one before it enters the register.

Contribute

Findings, corrections and counter-evidence are welcome from people and from AI agents acting for them. Every proposal is checked against its source, and a person decides whether it changes the register.

Three ways in

A lead from the field

Heard a figure at an event, on a call or in a community? Give the company, the claim and where you heard it. That is enough to start. Nine organizations in the register arrived this way, and their rows say who spotted them.

A finding with its source

The full record: who measured what, in whom and when, with a link to the original. People, vendors, AI labs and AI agents use the same format, set out below.

The weekly scan

Each Monday Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, scans earnings material, new research, industry news and the customer stories that vendors and AI labs publish, and files proposals in that format. It cannot change the register.

What a finding needs

FieldWhat to give
Organization or studyWho measured it or said it
FindingOne sentence, with the number and what it counts
Population and periodWho was measured or asked, and when
BasisObserved, self-reported, estimated or forecast. Add “vendor” when the source sells the product it measures, reports from its own platform’s data or surveys the market it sells to. A company reporting on its own operations stays self-reported
Proposed gradeA, B or C, by the grading method
SourceA link to the original document where one exists, not to coverage of it
Proposed byYour name. For an agent, the model and the person or organization it is acting for

A proposal as data

{
  "organization": "Example Co",
  "finding": "Support agent closed 58% of eligible tickets with no person involved; 9 in 10 sampled closures were confirmed resolved",
  "population_and_period": "Company disclosure, Q4 2026",
  "basis": "Self-reported (vendor)",
  "proposed_grade": "B",
  "sources": [{"label": "Company post", "url": "https://example.com/post"}],
  "proposed_by": {"name": "Agent or person", "model": "If an AI agent", "acting_for": "Person or organization"}
}

Example values, not a real finding. The fields match the register file.

How a proposal is handled

  1. Checked. Claude opens the source and confirms the number, its unit, the population, any comparison group and the dates of fieldwork and publication.
  2. Graded. The finding is graded by what it can prove, whatever grade was proposed.
  3. Flagged. A source that sells the product it measures, reports from its own platform’s data or surveys the market it sells to is marked as a vendor. A company reporting on its own operations is not.
  4. Decided. Nathan Fierley accepts or rejects each proposal from that check. When a company sends a correction to its own figure, he opens the source himself.
  5. Credited. An accepted finding names who spotted it, who compiled it, who checked its source and who edited it.
  6. Logged. Corrections to existing findings follow the same route, and a corrected row carries the date.
  7. Never paid. No one can pay to add, move or remove a finding, or to be described differently.

Contributions so far

99 records. Spotted: 63 by Claude in research, 25 by Nathan Fierley in the field, 7 by GPT-6.2 Astra in an outside review and 4 by Andy Jolls in the field. Compiled and checked against sources: all 99 by Claude. Rechecked: 53 by GPT-6.2 Astra on November 20, 2026. Corrected: 37 rows in all, 10 of them after that recheck. Edited: all 99 by Nathan Fierley. Proposals from outside: 31 from GPT-6.2 Astra, an AI model made by OpenAI, in an outside review on November 20, 2026, all accepted.

How to send a proposal. File it as an issue in the site’s public GitHub repository: propose a finding or report a correction. Each form asks for the fields above, and an AI agent can file one for the person it acts for. You can also send a proposal to Nathan Fierley on LinkedIn. Issues on GitHub are public.

Reading the site by machine

The whole site is one page that reads without scripts. Four files travel with it, and every file behind the site is public on GitHub.

  • evidence.json: the register, one record for each finding
  • llms.txt: a plain-text map of the site
  • robots.txt: open to search and AI crawlers
  • sitemap.xml: the site’s address for search engines

Reusing a figure

Keep the grade, the basis and the date with the number. Write “reports” for a self-reported figure. Cite the original source for the figure and Modern GTM for the grade. Terms for reusing the site’s own text, tables and tools are not set yet, so ask before republishing them. Each figure stays under its source’s terms.
