What is not listed

  • Partner plugins. Five more plugins in Anthropic's repository are built by partners: Apollo (built by Apollo.io), Common Room, Brand voice (Tribe AI), Slack (Salesforce) and Zoom, which is for developers who build Zoom integrations.
  • Other teams' plugins. Five of Anthropic's own are outside go-to-market (GTM) work: Engineering, Bio-research, Productivity, Plugin management and PDF viewer.
  • Google. Its skills in the Gemini app and in Google Workspace are reusable instructions that a team writes itself or adapts from a template. One search on November 21, 2026 found no set of sales skills built by Google.
  • Microsoft. Its documentation, last updated on November 3, 2026, describes two sales plugins for Copilot Cowork. Sales works with Dynamics 365 Sales and needs a license for it. Sales for Cowork needs no CRM license, and Microsoft calls it CRM-agnostic. Both also need a license for Microsoft Copilot, and Microsoft says Cowork is billed on usage. The documentation lists 18 skills by name: by our count of its table, 17 are in Sales and 6 in Sales for Cowork, with 5 in both. A Microsoft post of November 17, 2026 says an updated Sales plugin is generally available and counts more than 57 skills across its Sales and Customer Service plugins. The documentation names no public copy of the skills' files, and neither plugin has been installed here, so they have no page yet. Both pages were read on November 23, 2026.

A listing is never paid for, and it is not an endorsement. How these pages were put together

Anthropic's Sales plugin for Claude

Anthropic, the AI lab that makes Claude, is the vendor of this plugin. It gives Claude 36 skills for sales work. This entry sets out what each skill does, reads and can change, with nothing to install, and then how to configure the plugin for a company.

Browse the 36 skillsConfigure it for your company

Preview. The editor has changed some ratings. His review of the rest is still to come.Read against Sales plugin 2.1.0 by Claude on November 21, 2026For revenue leaders and operators

Compiled with Claude, an Anthropic model, from Anthropic's own files. On November 22, 2026 models from two other labs checked it against those files in two rounds, and on November 23, 2026 one of them checked the statements that had changed since. Claude made the corrections after each. The text as it now stands has had no check from outside. Its editor decides what is published.

What the plugin's files show

  1. 13 of the 36 skills read and propose.By their own steps they change nothing in a connected tool and send or post nothing. What one of them produces is shown in Claude, and it can be a page that others read, as the battlecards of competitive-intelligence are. A change one of them proposes is made by another skill, once you accept it or where a schedule was set up to make it. Every skill's file also carries one rule: an action you ask for goes through a connected tool. So this counts what each skill's own steps set up, by the furthest it goes in its own file. It is not a count of the most a skill can do.Our count from the files
  2. 22 go further by their own steps.Six can post to team chat. daily-briefing and weekly-wrap post their own output. The other four post a message drawn from it: account-context a note to an account's owner, lead-triage a lead handoff, team-pipeline its Monday questions for reps and rep-context a follow-up after a one-to-one. Three write for a customer and change no record. 13 list a change to a record in their own write line: a CRM update, a booked meeting or a contact added to a sequence. In all, six are written to email a customer: call-summary, inbox-sweep, schedule-meeting, draft-outreach, close-plan and handle-objection. Two more can email someone you name: daily-briefing sends its briefing to any address you give, and the request for missing information that route-lead drafts goes to whoever can supply it. Each acts when you ask, within the setting on the connector's tool. setup is counted apart: with write tools on, its dashboard's tiles carry write actions, and each runs when you click it.Our count from the files
  3. 22 other skills name one skill for record changes.That skill is update-opportunity: 21 hand their changes to it and route-lead follows its pattern. It is not the only writer. Eight others write on their own: schedule-meeting, log-activity, stakeholder-map, draft-outreach, route-lead, account-plan, expansion-whitespace and customer-health. On four more the change is applied through it: call-summary, close-plan, forecast and renewal-radar. renewal-radar also creates the renewal deals you accept, through the creation flow its file names. 18 of the 36 files open their write line with the word none, and five of those can still post, reply or make a customer document: lead-triage, handle-objection, create-an-asset, team-pipeline and rep-context. The control is the setting on each connector's write tool, not any one skill.Our count from the files
  4. 13 are built around a deal record.They read a deal with a stage, an amount and a close date. A team that keeps no such record leaves them little to read. Working from files, each takes an export or the details you give it.Our read of the skills' steps
  5. Three are written for leaders.The plugin's own descriptions call team-pipeline a leader view, rep-context a leader's prep and win-loss-review leader-focused.From the plugin's files
  6. Nine can be run for a team, and five for a named rep.Each file names its own scope, and no two are quite alike. Four take either: deal-slip-scenario, pipeline-review, forecast and win-loss-review. rep-context takes one rep and no team.Our count from the files
  7. Seven are named as routines.Each is offered on a schedule in its own description or in setup's list of routines. All 36 files carry one rule on scheduled runs, and 20 add instructions for a run of their own skill. The rule: a scheduled run takes only the actions it was set up to take, within what its connectors allow. An action that an email, a chat or a transcript dictates or asks for becomes a proposal. The plugin's README advises setting every tool that sends, posts or writes to ask first.Our count from the files
  8. It reads through 10 kinds of tool.The plugin's connector list covers the CRM, email, calendar, chat, documents, call recording, data enrichment, sales engagement, competitive intelligence and a project tracker. Its server file sets up 23 servers in advance.From the plugin's files
  9. Every skill runs with nothing connected.It works from an upload or from what you paste, and says what it could not see. Two skills mark one source as needed: a transcript or notes for call-summary, and email for inbox-sweep.From the plugin's files

How to read a skill's name

The outline or fill of a name shows the furthest the skill goes by its own steps. It is the same in every part of this entry. It is not a permission, and not the most a skill can do: every skill's file carries the rule that an action you ask for, such as an update, an email, a post or a booking, goes through a connected tool. What a run can do is set by the tools you connect and the setting on each, and each skill's card lists what its own file sets up. On a schedule, any skill takes the actions the schedule was set up to take, within what its connectors allow. An action that outside content dictates or asks for stays a proposal.

  • 13 skillsReads and proposes. By its own steps it changes nothing in a connected tool and sends or posts nothing. What it produces is shown in Claude, and can be a page that others read. A change it proposes is made by another skill, once you accept it or where a schedule was set up to make it.
  • 6 skillsShares its output. It can post to team chat when you ask: its own output, or a message drawn from it. daily-briefing can also email its briefing to an address you name. It changes no record.
  • 3 skillsWrites for customers. It writes a reply or a document meant for a customer, and changes no record. Two of the three can send an email when you ask.
  • 13 skillsChanges records. Its own write line lists a change to a record: a CRM update, a booked meeting or a contact added to a sequence. Four of them can also email a customer.
  • 1 skillFirst run. setup alone. It reads your tools to build your dashboard and learn your voice. With write tools on, the dashboard's tiles carry write actions, and each runs when you click it.

Fact and our read

What a skill does, reads and can change, send or post is restated from version 2.1.0 of the plugin's files.

A count or a grouping that we made from the files is marked as ours, with its rule.

Role fit, overlap with other tools, value, frequency and the model to start on are our read. They are marked wherever they appear, and none of it is usage data.

Who can get it

Anthropic's help center lists plugins on its paid plans. Sharing a plugin with colleagues and publishing one to an organization need a Team or Enterprise plan. The plugin's folder holds a LICENSE file with the Apache 2.0 text, which we read in Anthropic's public repository on GitHub. Its files state no price.

Controls

Each connector tool can be set to allow, ask first or block. The plugin's files tell Claude to stay inside those settings, to make a change you ask for and to show a change it proposes before making it. Those are instructions to a model. The setting on the tool is the control. The files do not describe how the provider stores or uses customer data.

What the provider reports

No result with a number appears in the plugin's files.

Evidence in the register

None yet.

Not public or not known

We found no usage data for the plugin in its files or on Anthropic's pages about it, read on November 21, 2026. How the skills perform against a live CRM, and how often each is used, are not known to us.

On this site

This entry's four parts: the skills, fit by role, sales motion and week, what to settle before rollout and how to configure it. The agent charter and the launch checklist under Tools also apply to skills that run on a schedule. All plugins lists this one beside the others.

Last checked

November 21, 2026, for the plugin's README, connector notes and 36 skill files, and for Anthropic's pages on Salesforce in Claude and Claude for Sales. November 16, 2026, for the configuration half and the help pages it cites.

Sales plugin
The subject of this entry. It comes from Anthropic, has 36 skills and works with whichever CRM you connect.
Salesforce in Claude
A separate plugin built with Salesforce, in beta since September 15, 2026, with 37 skills of its own. It is not covered here.
Claude for Sales
The title of Anthropic's solutions page for sales teams, which groups both plugins with other features.

As Anthropic's own pages describe them on November 21, 2026.

setup, the first run.First run: what is connected, your voice and a starter dashboard

First run. It checks which tools answer, says what each one unlocks, works out your role and book from the CRM, and builds a starter dashboard with no interview. Where two tools answer for the same job, such as two mailboxes, it takes the one on your CRM's email domain and asks one question only if that does not settle it. It also asks once if colleagues appear on a second email domain.

Voice and signature (it learns this from your sent mail, or from 5 to 10 emails you paste, and does not ask for it).
Worth knowing
It learns your voice from 30 to 60 sent emails, or 5 to 10 pasted ones, after it drops duplicates and strips quoted replies and forwarded headers. Below five usable emails it says the voice is not learned and does not guess. Where Microsoft 365 mail is connected read-only, it says after the first refusal that drafts will come as text to paste until an admin turns the write tools on.

Which skills fit your team

The plugin locks no skill to a role, and the same skill is a daily habit in one business and idle in another. Choose a role and the sales motion closest to yours.

This part is our read from the skill files, apart from the lines marked as from the files. None of it is usage data. It was compiled with Claude, an Anthropic model, about an Anthropic plugin. Its editor has changed some of the ratings, and his review of the rest is still to come.

By role

Where it can read the CRM, the plugin's setup skill infers one of four roles: account executive, SDR or BDR, leader or customer success. With a role or without one, it suggests three skills to start with. The rows below are a wider reading, role by role.

Built for this role means the skill does that role's own core work. Also useful means it helps now and then. setup is each person's own run, leaders included: first on opening the plugin, and again to check what is connected or to relearn a voice. So no row lists it.

What separates a rep's skill from a manager's

  • Three skills are written for leadersThe plugin's own descriptions call team-pipeline a leader view, rep-context a leader's prep and win-loss-review leader-focused.
  • Nine can be run for a team, and five for a named repEach file names its own scope, and each works within what the person running it can see. For a team: weekly-wrap, deal-signals, deal-slip-scenario, pipeline-review, forecast, team-pipeline, win-loss-review, customer-voice and renewal-radar. For a named rep: deal-slip-scenario, pipeline-review, forecast, rep-context and win-loss-review.
  • Access follows the personClaude acts with each person's own sign-in, so a manager sees a team only as far as the CRM already allows. rep-context leaves out what the manager cannot see, and says so.
  • Leaders mostly need three viewsThe number: forecast, team-pipeline and deal-slip-scenario. The patterns: win-loss-review, competitive-intelligence and customer-voice. The base: renewal-radar.

The first and third come from the plugin's files and Anthropic's help pages. The second is our count from the files, and the fourth is our read.

Five skills are used when something calls for them, so the table gives no frequency for them. stakeholder-map: when you need to see who matters in a deal or an account. deal-slip-scenario: when a deal, or a few, may slip, shrink or be lost, and the number is at stake. close-plan: when a deal is in its late stages. create-an-asset: when a customer or an internal audience needs a document or a deck made for them. customer-health: before a business review, or when an account feels off.

How to read a rating

  • Core. Close to how the skill was written.
  • Useful. Works, with part of it idle.
  • Occasional. A narrow case, or it needs data this motion rarely keeps.
  • Poor fit. Built around a record or a process this motion usually lacks.
  • Frequency. How often the person a skill suits would reach for it: daily, weekly, monthly, or quarterly or less. It is a first guess from how the skill is designed. A poor fit is given none.
  • Outside the grid. setup is each person's own setup run, so it is not placed.

Through the week

A skill becomes a habit when it has a fixed moment. The first list sorts the skills rated core or useful for the chosen role and sales motion by how often they are likely to be used, with those used only when something calls for them at the end. The routines under it put a few skills in the order a day calls for them.

The routines and their order are ours, as a suggested way to work. Each step after the first is tied to the one before it by a line in one of the two skills' files: a handoff, a suggestion or a named source. The step says which, with the condition the file gives.

Eight routines

Each step shows the skill and what to say. Brackets mark the part you fill in.

Around a customer call

Every meeting with a customer. For SDR or BDR, account executive, account manager or CSM, and founder or full-cycle seller.

  1. call-prep, reads and proposesPrep me for my meeting with [account].
  2. call-summary, changes recordsSummarize my call with [account] and draft the follow-up.Suggested by call-prep: when a live calendar shows the meeting has ended.
  3. log-activity, changes recordsLog my [call] with [account].Handed on by call-summary.
  4. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by log-activity: for a next step on the deal.

A new lead

When a lead arrives. For SDR or BDR, founder or full-cycle seller, and RevOps or enablement.

Score it and reach out

  1. lead-triage, can share its outputTriage this lead: [paste the lead].
  2. draft-outreach, changes recordsDraft outreach to [person] at [company].Suggested by lead-triage: as one first touch.
  3. log-activity, changes recordsLog that I emailed [contact].Handed on by draft-outreach: to log the email, if you want it logged.

Give it an owner, on a team that assigns leads

  1. lead-triage, can share its outputTriage this lead: [paste the lead].
  2. route-lead, changes recordsRoute this lead: [paste the lead].Takes lead-triage's output: the triage verdict.

The two files differ on one case: an account that has an owner, with an open deal owned by someone else. lead-triage says to coordinate with the account's owner. route-lead gives the lead to the deal's owner. Write your own rule down before the two are used together.

The end of the day

Daily, before you stop. For SDR or BDR, account executive, account manager or CSM, and founder or full-cycle seller.

Close out today

  1. end-of-day, reads and proposesClose out my day.
  2. call-summary, changes recordsSummarize my call with [account] and draft the follow-up.Handed on by end-of-day: for each call you choose to process.
  3. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by call-summary: for the changes you accept.

Set up tomorrow

  1. end-of-day, reads and proposesClose out my day.
  2. call-prep, reads and proposesPrep me for my meeting with [account].Suggested by end-of-day: for tomorrow's first meeting.

Forecast week

The days before a forecast call. For account executive, founder or full-cycle seller, frontline manager, and sales leader.

Clean the records first

  1. crm-hygiene-check, reads and proposesCheck my CRM hygiene.
  2. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by crm-hygiene-check: for the fixes you accept.

Then build the call

  1. forecast, changes recordsWrite my forecast for [this quarter].
  2. deal-slip-scenario, reads and proposesWhat happens to my number if [deal] slips to next quarter?Handed on by forecast: for a deal that may slip.
  3. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by deal-slip-scenario: for a date or category change that comes out of it.

A manager's week

Before the team's pipeline review and each one-to-one. For frontline manager and sales leader.

The team's pipeline

  1. team-pipeline, can share its outputShow my team's pipeline.
  2. pipeline-review, reads and proposesReview my team's pipeline.Handed on by team-pipeline: for the full at-risk list.
  3. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by pipeline-review.

Before a one-to-one

  1. team-pipeline, can share its outputShow my team's pipeline.
  2. rep-context, can share its outputPrep me for my one-to-one with [rep].Handed on by team-pipeline: for one rep's detail.

A deal that has stalled

When a deal has sat in one stage. For account executive and founder or full-cycle seller.

  1. deal-advance-gap, reads and proposesWhat is missing to advance the [account] deal?
  2. close-plan, changes recordsBuild a close plan for the [account] deal.Takes deal-advance-gap's output: the gaps it found, when both run in one conversation.
  3. update-opportunity, changes recordsUpdate [deal]: [the change, such as a new close date].Handed on by close-plan.

A competitor in the deal

When a customer names a competitor. For account executive and founder or full-cycle seller.

  1. competitive-intelligence, reads and proposesHow do we beat [competitor] in the [account] deal?
  2. handle-objection, writes for customersThey said: [the objection]. How do I respond?Suggested by competitive-intelligence: for a specific pushback.
  3. draft-outreach, changes recordsDraft outreach to [person] at [company].Handed on by handle-objection: for the written reply, by its write line.

A renewal in view

Some months ahead of a renewal date. For account manager or CSM and founder or full-cycle seller.

Read the account

  1. renewal-radar, changes recordsWhat renewals are coming up?
  2. customer-health, changes recordsHow healthy is [account]?Draws on renewal-radar: for how close the renewal is.

Look for growth

  1. renewal-radar, changes recordsWhat renewals are coming up?
  2. expansion-whitespace, changes recordsWhere can I expand [account]?Handed on by renewal-radar: for the full pass on growth.

Before you roll it out

A rep can get into trouble with a good skill by using it in place of the system the business bought for that job. The plugin does not know what else you own. Two checks come before a rollout: where each skill meets a tool you already run, and whether your records give it enough to read. One setting comes with them, which is the model a skill runs on.

Compiled with Claude, an Anthropic model, about an Anthropic plugin. The sorting and the model advice in this part are our read. The editor has changed some of both, and his review of the rest is still to come.

The ruleThis plugin, sortedReadiness checkWhich modelEight setups

A rule for any assistant that can act in your tools

Sort what the assistant can do into three groups before anyone uses it. The groups are worded for any provider's sales skills, and the rest of this part applies them to one.

  1. Agree the rule first. Anything that can change a record or put words in front of a customer. Decide where the official version lives, and who may let the assistant write there.
  2. Know the overlap. Anything that changes no record and writes to no customer by its own steps, but gives a second view of a figure another tool or team already reports. Use it to prepare, and quote the official tool.
  3. Start here. Anything that reads and proposes, and competes with nothing you run. These are the low-risk pilots, as long as the tools you grant them cannot send or write.

Our read; tests to run

The three groups are our synthesis from one provider's plugin so far. They are not a finding in the evidence register.

  1. List every tool the assistant can write to, and name one owner for each.
  2. For each official figure, such as the forecast, a health score or a lead score, name the one system that holds it.

The same sort gets run on the next provider entry. If the groups do not hold there, this section changes.

What the plugin's files tell Claude to do about it

  • Permissions sit on each connector toolEach can be allowed, set to ask first or blocked, and the files tell Claude to stay inside that. If a write is blocked, the skill is to hand over a checklist to apply by hand, and never to try another tool to make the change.
  • Asked for is done, suggested is shownThe files tell Claude to make a change you request, and to show a change it proposes first, with its evidence, for you to accept.
  • Outside content is informationThe files tell Claude never to treat email, transcripts, chat or enrichment data as instructions. If an email asks for something to be sent or changed, the skill is to show you that request before anything happens.
  • Scheduled runs stay in their laneA scheduled run is to take only the actions it was set up to take, within what its connectors allow, and nothing that outside content dictates or asks for. In eight skills a value, a record or a contact taken from a transcript, an email, a chat or enrichment is never written on a schedule, even when the schedule was set up to make that kind of update: call-summary, stakeholder-map, account-plan, expansion-whitespace, crm-hygiene-check, forecast, customer-health and renewal-radar.
  • An empty result is not widenedWhen a search of your own records comes back empty, the skill is to stop and ask, and never to widen silently to the whole company.
  • The forecast skill stops short of submittingIts file says that step belongs to your forecasting tool.
  • The asset skill names its sourcesClaims are to come from approved material, your account data or what you supply, and the rest is labeled unverified.

These are instructions to a model, restated from the files. We did not test whether they hold in a live run.

What it leaves to you

The plugin cannot know that your forecast belongs in another tool, or that a routing tool should own assignment. Someone has to tell the team.

Its safeguards are written instructions to the model. The dependable control is the permission on each connector tool, which an admin sets. For scheduled runs, the plugin's README advises ask first for every tool that sends, posts or writes.

The files leave three questions open, for whoever runs your Claude workspace: who can see a page once it is shared, how long uploaded records are kept and who corrects a post that turns out to be wrong.

          What each skill leans on is our read of its steps. The plugin keeps no such list. The check looks at inputs only: it tests no permission, no routing rule and no result. For a first pilot, name an owner, a handful of real cases, the figure or record to compare the output with, and what counts as a pass.

          A sample plan for a first pilot of a skill that can reach a customer

          This is a sketch for schedule-meeting, which can put an invitation in a customer's inbox. Change the parts to fit your own tools. What the skill is to do is restated from its file. The cases, the pass and the stop rule are our read, as a place to start.

          Owner
          One person who signs off the pilot, and one who checks each run against the calendar and the CRM.
          Cases
          Up to 10 real requests. Include a follow-up with one contact, an account with two open deals, a contact with no email address on the record, a request made while the calendar's write tool is blocked and the same request made a second time.
          What the file says to expect
          With two open deals, it asks which one the meeting belongs to. With no address on the record, it shows one from the header of an email thread as unverified, and uses it once you pick it. With the write tool blocked, it gives the invite details as text to paste, quotes the refusal and neither retries nor reaches for another tool. The file does not say what happens when you ask a second time, so check for a duplicate.
          What to compare
          After a direct booking, the calendar: one event at the time agreed, 30 minutes long, or 60 for a demo or a quarterly business review, unless you said otherwise, with attendees taken only from your own words, the CRM or an address you picked from a thread. The customer's inbox: one invitation, since creating the event emails every attendee. The CRM, when you asked for the meeting to be logged or booked end to end: one event or activity on the related deal or account, saved as it was shown.
          Who puts it right
          Name who corrects a wrong invitation or a duplicate record, and who tells the customer.
          A pass
          Every case gives the result its kind calls for. A direct booking: right on all three counts above. A blocked write: the invite details as text to paste, and nothing created in the calendar, the inbox or the CRM. Two open deals: it asks which one and waits for your answer. No address on the record: it uses only an address you picked. A repeat: count what was created, since the file sets no check for duplicates. A wrong attendee fails the case, whatever else is right.
          When to stop
          At a wrong attendee, a meeting logged to the wrong deal or a booking made while the tool was blocked. Find the cause before the next run.
          Not known until you measure it
          The time a booking saves, how long an approval takes with the tools set to ask first, what it costs and whether more meetings are held.

Better with: logged activity; stage history; email; call recordings or notes; renewal dates. Note: Working from files, it needs the export before this one as well, to show what changed.

Without that, an export or a paste. Better with: reporting lines; team chat. May ask about: forecast categories; quota.

Note: It judges value delivered against documented outcomes and a success plan, where one exists.

          Which model to run a skill on

          The plugin does not choose a model. None of its 36 skill files names one, so a skill runs on whichever model is selected in Claude at the moment you ask. The model is a setting for your team to decide, and it changes three things: how much a skill catches, how long you wait and what the reply looks like.

          What Anthropic says

          • Opus 5.5 is the usual place to startAnthropic's guide to choosing a model starts most work there.
          • Sonnet 5.5 for everyday workThe guide pairs it with speed: writing, analysis and agent tasks of an ordinary day.
          • Haiku 5.5 for volumeIt has the lowest latency and price, and suits high-volume and real-time work.
          • Fable 5.2 at the topThe guide calls it the most capable model open to all customers, and points it at long agent sessions and deep research.
          • Effort is a second dialWithin one model, an effort setting trades quality against time and cost. The guide's advice is to try that dial first, since it often does more than a change of model.

          From Anthropic's guide to choosing a model, read on November 21, 2026. Anthropic is the vendor, and the guide is written for developers. It does not mention the plugin.

          What the plugin's files say

          Nothing about models. No skill file names a model or an effort level, and neither does the README or the connector list.

          The files do describe what comes back, and they tie it to what is connected: a rendered page where one helps, and paste-ready text or a checklist where the skill cannot write.

          A rule to start from

          Sort each skill by what a mistake would cost and by how much judgment it needs. This is our read as of November 2026, and model names date quickly.

          • It changes records or writes for customers

            A slip costs more than a few seconds of waiting. Start on the stronger model, with every tool it can write or send through set to ask first. This rests on what an error would cost, and it is unmeasured: the test below did not cover writes.

            Opus 5.5 to start, 16 skills

            call-summary, changes recordsinbox-sweep, writes for customersschedule-meeting, changes recordslog-activity, changes recordsstakeholder-map, changes recordsdraft-outreach, changes recordsroute-lead, changes recordsaccount-plan, changes recordsexpansion-whitespace, changes recordsclose-plan, changes recordshandle-objection, writes for customerscreate-an-asset, writes for customersupdate-opportunity, changes recordsforecast, changes recordscustomer-health, changes recordsrenewal-radar, changes records

          • It weighs several sources and makes a call

            A review, a diagnosis or a pattern across many deals. The one skill of this kind in the test below scored the same on every model, so the rule starts these on the faster model. That rests on one skill, run once.

            Sonnet 5.5 to start, 7 skills

            deal-review, reads and proposesdeal-advance-gap, reads and proposescompetitive-intelligence, reads and proposespipeline-review, reads and proposesteam-pipeline, can share its outputwin-loss-review, reads and proposescustomer-voice, reads and proposes

          • A scoped job with a clear input

            One account, one meeting or one question.

            Sonnet 5.5 to start, 11 skills

            setup, the first rundaily-briefing, can share its outputcall-prep, reads and proposesend-of-day, reads and proposesweekly-wrap, can share its outputaccount-research, reads and proposesaccount-context, can share its outputlead-triage, can share its outputaccount-tiering, reads and proposesdeal-slip-scenario, reads and proposesrep-context, can share its output

          • A repeated pass that returns a list you can check

            The same check on every deal, often on a schedule. Try the smallest model once a run has matched your own rules and records.

          Fable 5.2 sits above all four rows. Keep it for the few jobs that run rarely and read a great deal, such as win-loss-review or account-plan, when a wait of several minutes is acceptable. We did not test it on either of those two.

          A small test

          We ran six of the skills on four Claude models, once each, on invented files that hold known answers. It is a pilot: 24 runs in all, enough to show where to look and too few to settle anything.

          • The filesOne invented company: a pipeline export of 24 deals, three call transcripts, an inbox of 10 messages, 12 inbound leads and a page of company facts. Problems were planted in them, such as three deals past their close date and an email that asks for a contract amount to be changed.
          • The runsOn November 21, 2026, each model got the same skill file, the same request and the same files in a session of its own, with no tool connected. Effort was left at each model's default.
          • The markingTwo separate Claude sessions marked each reply against the answer key. They saw the replies under code names and were not told which model wrote which.
          • What was markedPlanted items found, numbers right and guardrails kept, such as promising no go-live date in a customer email and claiming no write that did not happen. Time and length were recorded by the run.
          ModelPlanted items foundNumbers in the key rightGuardrails keptSlips the markers notedTime for one runWhat came back
          Haiku 5.566.25 of 6810 of 1019 of 21Kept a skill's default over the company's rule. Credited a competitor's claim to the customer. Both cost marks.45 s to 79 sA short reply with a separate page or document in one of six runs, and everything in one reply in the other five. 638 to 1,353 words in all.
          Sonnet 5.568 of 6810 of 1021 of 21One wrong total in a summary table. It is outside the key, so no mark was lost.28 s to 54 sA short reply with a separate page or document in four of six runs, and everything in one reply in the other two. 1,009 to 1,586 words in all.
          Opus 5.568 of 6810 of 1021 of 21Two wrong figures in one caveat. They are outside the key, so no mark was lost.61 s to 1 min 59 sA short reply with a separate page or document, every time. 1,553 to 2,270 words in all.
          Fable 5.268 of 6810 of 1021 of 21None found.12 min 56 s to 20 min 05 sA short reply with a separate page or document, every time. 2,055 to 3,109 words in all.

          Summed over the six skills. An item's mark is the mean of two markers, and a partly found item counts as half. One item of the key was wrong and was corrected on November 22, 2026, which raised each model's total by half a mark. The numbers column counts only the figures in the key. The slips column says of each slip whether it cost a mark: the two by Haiku 5.5 did, and the figures that Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 added sit outside the key. Time runs from a session's first step to its last, in our test harness and not in the Claude app.

          What the test suggests

          • The planted problems did not separate the three larger modelsSonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 each found all 68. Haiku 5.5 found 66.25. Every number in the key was right. On work this well defined, from clean files, the three tied and the smallest model came close.
          • Speed was the widest gapOne run took Sonnet 5.5 under a minute and Haiku 5.5 little more. Opus 5.5 took 1 to 2 minutes. Fable 5.2 took 13 to 20 minutes and made several times as many tool calls. A wait of that length suits a quarterly review, not a skill used daily.
          • The slips were in the detailsHaiku 5.5 kept the hygiene skill's 14-day default where the company's own rule said 30 days, and in a call summary it credited a competitor's claim to the customer. Sonnet 5.5 got one total wrong in a summary table, and Opus 5.5 got an amount and a ratio wrong in one caveat. Both were figures the models added beyond the request, so neither cost a mark. The markers found no such slip in Fable 5.2's six replies.
          • The guardrails mostly heldAll four models showed the rep an email that asked for a contract amount to be changed, and none acted on it. None claimed a write or a send, and none named the competitor to the customer. One Haiku 5.5 draft put the customer's go-live date in writing, against the company's rule.
          • One skill came back in different shapesOpus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 gave a short reply with a separate page or document every time. Haiku 5.5 put everything into one long reply in five runs of six. Sonnet 5.5 did each. The model shapes the output as well as the skill does.
          • What it does to the starting ruleIt supports Sonnet 5.5 for scoped and repeated work: on these six it scored the same as Opus 5.5 in about half the time. It supports checking a Haiku 5.5 run against your own rules before trusting it. It gave no measured reason to start a skill that weighs several sources on Opus 5.5: the one skill of that kind we tested, pipeline-review, scored the same on every model. So since November 23, 2026 the rule starts those seven on Sonnet 5.5, by the editor's decision. The other tested skill that only reads, crm-hygiene-check, is a repeated pass, where Haiku 5.5 found 14 of 15 items and the other three found all 15. Nor does the test give a reason to prefer Fable 5.2. On skills that can write it says nothing, because nothing was connected. We keep Opus 5.5 for those as a place to start and step down from. That rests on what a mistake would cost, not on a difference we measured.

          What it does not show

          • One run each. A second run could come out differently, so no single result means much.
          • Too easy at the top. The planted problems could not tell three of the four models apart. A harder test would plant conflicts between sources and calls that need judgment.
          • From files only. Nothing was connected, so no write, no send and no live record was tested. That is where a wrong choice of model costs most.
          • A test harness, not the Claude app. Effort was whatever each session defaulted to, and Anthropic's guide lists a higher default for Fable 5.2 and Sonnet 5.5 than for Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. Times in the app will differ.
          • One vendor's models marked each other. Two Claude sessions marked every reply separately, and on that first marking they agreed on 390 of 396 marks. The answer key is made of checkable facts, and the slips named above were checked by hand against the test files.
          • Two flaws in our own test, one now corrected. One line of the invented company's stage rules can be read two ways. Three models read it one way and Fable 5.2 the other, and the key counted neither. The key also expected a draft reply to a set of legal redlines, where the skill's own file says to flag legal mail and not draft it. All four models flagged it, and the first marking took half a mark from each. A model from another lab caught the error on November 22, 2026. The totals here count the item as found. The markers' own marks are kept with the files, and the corrected mark was set by Claude, not by the two markers.

          Eight setups worth checking

          We do not call them opportunities
          The skills take stage and field names from your CRM instead of assuming one vendor's. HubSpot's deals, for example, are checked on their own properties. From an upload, a skill uses your own column headers.
          Our deals live in a custom object
          Nothing in the skill files describes standing in another object for deals. Expect to say so in your project instructions, or to work from an export. This is our read of the files and was not tested.
          We do not track deals at all
          Thirteen skills are built around a deal with a stage, an amount and a close date, and have little to read without one: weekly-wrap, deal-review, deal-advance-gap, deal-signals, deal-slip-scenario, close-plan, update-opportunity, pipeline-review, crm-hygiene-check, forecast, team-pipeline, rep-context and win-loss-review. That grouping is ours. Others lose a part: account-context names its deals section as having no data, daily-briefing shows leads in that row when you upload a lead backlog, and competitive-intelligence loses its counts of wins and losses.
          We log client meetings as events
          Two skills check this for themselves. log-activity reads from the CRM whether meetings are logged as tasks or as calendar-style events, and schedule-meeting whether they are calendar-style events or activities. Each drafts the shape your setup expects.
          Our renewals are not deals
          renewal-radar accepts renewal deals, contract records or a renewal date field. It reads which you use from the CRM and from what it already knows about your company, and asks once only if neither tells it.
          Our customers are households
          lead-triage marks industry and company size as not applicable for a consumer lead, and scores the dimensions that do apply. Scoring on intent alone is its rule for a team with no ICP recorded. account-research and account-tiering score fit on industry, size and buyer titles, so they have less to go on.
          Our meeting notes sit in a shared drive
          Four skills say that the Google Drive connector cannot see shared drives, or may not: setup, call-prep, call-summary and customer-voice. Each is to name the gap and offer a paste or an upload. Notes kept there are missed until you paste or upload them.
          We run on Salesforce and Microsoft 365
          Both are included. Each needs an admin to enable it before anyone can sign in.

          Configure it for your company

          Out of the box, the Claude Sales plugin knows nothing about your company, so its skills infer what they can, fall back on a labeled default or ask. Configure it once and they work from your ICP, your stages and your wording rules. This guide starts with what you get, role by role, then shows how to set it up.

          A plugin that already knows your company

          A configured Sales plugin starts from your company's facts and works your way. Each stock skill lists the company facts it needs and looks for them in your connected tools and instructions. When a fact is missing, the skill infers it from what it can read or uses a labeled default, and asks one question where the answer would change the result. It keeps that answer for the conversation only. Configuration writes those answers down once.

          You askStock pluginConfigured plugin
          Triage this inbound leadWith no ideal customer written down, scores on intent alone. Asks about it only if the answer would change the priority.Scores against your written ICP and disqualifiers, and names your handoff channel.
          Prep me for tomorrow's callUses your CRM's stage names, and asks which qualification method you run.Builds discovery questions around your qualification method.
          Draft a follow-upWrites in your voice if it has learned it, then by a style guide you uploaded or your sent mail where it can read it, otherwise in a neutral one. Knows no company wording rules.Follows your messaging rules, approved proof points and signature.
          Write my forecastUses the CRM's own forecast category where it has one. Otherwise infers the categories from your stages, and asks which stages count as commit only if the answer depends on it.Uses your mapping of stages to forecast categories, where the CRM has no forecast category of its own.
          Which renewals are coming up?Reads where renewal dates live from the CRM and from what it already knows about your company, and asks once only if neither tells it.Reads the field you named.

          This comparison comes from reading what each stock skill asks for. It is not a benchmark.

          What configuration buys you

          • Fewer repeated questionsA stock answer lasts one conversation. A configured fact is there every time, for every skill that needs it.
          • The same rules for everyoneEvery seller's skills use one ICP, one set of stage definitions and one set of wording rules.
          • Guardrails that travelA rule such as "no pricing by email" is given to every draft, whoever asks for it. It is an instruction to the model. A tool permission can block every send or hold each one for a yes. It cannot check what an email says, so a rule about content still needs a person's review.
          • Honest gapsWhere your company has not decided something, the configuration can say so. The skill then reports the gap instead of inventing a rule.

          What it does not do

          Configuration does not clean a messy CRM or settle a sales process you have not decided. It makes the plugin repeat your decisions, good or bad.

          This guide makes no claims about time saved or deals won. The benefits above are how the plugin is designed to behave. Measure the results on your own team before you quote them.

          The example lines are invented for a fictional company. They show the level of detail that works: one decision, stated plainly.

          What the stock plugin already does by role

          The plugin adapts to the person before you configure anything. Its setup skill infers a role from the CRM: AE, BDR or SDR, leader, or customer success. It then builds a role-aware dashboard and recommends three skills to start with. Three skills, team-pipeline, rep-context and win-loss-review, are written for leaders.

          Where configuration differs by role

          • Emphasis. Every role shares the same facts, but each stresses different ones. Configure first the rows for the roles you actually have.
          • Handoffs. Configuration pays most where work changes hands. Lead to AE needs routing rules and a handoff note. AE to account manager needs renewal dates and products recorded at close.
          • The personal layer. Voice, signature, book and territory belong to one person. Let setup learn them, and keep them in that person's own instructions, not the shared plugin.
          • Access. Owners on Team and Enterprise plans set tool permissions for the whole organization. Claude also acts with each person's own access in the CRM, so your CRM roles still apply.

          One build or several

          Keep one build unless two teams truly sell differently. One build means one set of facts to maintain, and the skills already serve every role.

          Separate builds drift apart, and each is another plugin to update. If two segments run different stages or messaging, split by segment, not by job title. Enterprise admins can then set which groups get which plugin.

          Admin, operator, seller: who changes what

          Roles decide which skills and facts matter. Seats decide who is allowed to change them. Three people shape a configuration, and each controls a different part of it.

          On a plan of your own you hold all three seats, and nothing here conflicts. On a Team or Enterprise plan the seats are usually different people, so read yours first.

          The admin

          Decide what each tool may do.

          An Owner or Primary Owner of the Claude organization. On Enterprise, also anyone whose custom role manages the organization's libraries. The role labeled Admin in the members list does not open the plugin settings.

          You control

          • Which connectors the organization has. Each member still signs in with their own account.
          • Tool permissions for everyone: always allow, needs approval or blocked. Members cannot loosen them.
          • Each plugin's availability: not available, available to install, installed by default or required. On Enterprise, by group.
          • What members may do themselves: create or upload plugins, share them, and publish them with or without review.

          You do not write

          • The sales facts. They belong to the operator.
          • Your settings decide who gets the build and what it may do.

          Your first move

          1. Add the connectors the plugin uses in organization settings. Making a plugin available does not add its connectors.
          2. Allow reads, put sends, posts and CRM writes on approval, and block what must never run.
          3. Decide the publishing policy before the operator submits anything.
          4. When the configured build arrives, set its availability, and decide whether the stock Sales plugin stays visible beside it.

          Watch for

          • "Installed by default" can be turned off by a member. "Required" cannot.
          • A group's setting replaces the organization's for that group, and the most permissive setting wins across several groups.
          • Items shared by someone who has left keep working until you stop the sharing.
          • In Claude Code, a same-named plugin someone installed themselves loads in place of the copy synced from the organization.

          The operator

          Write the company facts down once.

          Whoever owns the sales process and its tools: revenue operations, sales operations, enablement, or a sales leader or founder doing that job.

          You control

          • The company facts and skill behavior. This is the build.
          • The reference page and the list of open decisions.
          • What goes to review, and when.
          • The update each time a source document changes.

          You depend on

          • The admin, for connectors, tool permissions and who receives the plugin.
          • Sellers, for how deals are really worked.
          • A reviewer's approval for each version, where publishing needs review.

          Your first move

          1. Gather the source documents and name the open decisions.
          2. Customize a copy and review it like a contract.
          3. Try it with a few sellers by sharing it with them directly.
          4. Publish it to the organization, and agree with the admin who gets it.

          Watch for

          • Sellers' private copies and instructions drifting from yours. Collect the good parts, then ask them to retire the copies.
          • Wording rules that clash with personal voice. Say in the build that company rules win.
          • An update that never arrives. A published plugin changes only when you publish it again.

          The seller

          Use the company build, and add your voice.

          An individual contributor using Claude on the company's plan.

          You control

          • Your sign-in to each tool. Claude acts with your access, so it sees the CRM records you can see.
          • Your voice, signature and role, which setup learns.
          • Your own project instructions and your scheduled routines.
          • Your own plugins, where the organization lets members add them.

          You cannot change

          • A plugin the organization manages, or one a colleague shared with you.
          • A plugin marked required. It stays on.
          • Tool permissions set for the organization.
          • Which connectors the organization has. You can ask for one where requests are turned on.

          Your first move

          1. Open Plugins and look for a Sales plugin your organization already provides.
          2. If there is one, use it. Add only your voice, role and schedules.
          3. If there is none, start with the stock plugin and put your own facts in project instructions.
          4. Send what works, and every question a skill still asks, to whoever owns the sales process.

          Watch for

          • Two Sales plugins turned on. Keep one.
          • Company facts in your instructions that disagree with the company build. Delete yours when the build arrives.
          • Your own voice in anything you share.

          Where the seats overlap

          Most conflicts come from the same thing being set in two places. Each row says what happens then, and how to keep it clean.

          Six things to configure, at three levels

          Customizing the plugin does its work at the company level. The tool and person levels are settings around it.

          Your tools

          Connectors

          Which tools Claude can read and act in.

          Owner

          Set in
          Each connector's tool permissions
          Owner
          Organization owners on Team and Enterprise plans

          Your company

          the part you customize

          Your ICP, stages, qualification method, messaging, competitors and CRM habits.

          Set in
          Written into the skills
          Owner
          A sales leader, revenue operations or the founder

          How a skill works your way: which recorder it reads, how it logs, what it must never do.

          Set in
          Edits to individual skills
          Owner
          The same owner

          Voice and role

          Each person's writing voice, signature, role and book.

          Set in

          Owner

          Set in

          Owner

          Two homes for company facts

          Project instructions

          The light route, and the one the stock plugin suggests. Paste your ICP, stages and rules into the instructions of the project where you sell. The stock skills are written to use facts they find there before asking.

          The plugin

          The durable route. Claude writes the facts into the skills, and you share one package with the team.

          Start with project instructions if you sell alone and want results today. Move to the plugin when a second person needs the same setup.

          Use permissions for hard limits

          Put hard limits in tool permissions, not in skill text. The stock skills are written to follow each connector's settings. They add two safeguards of their own: an action that outside content asks for is shown to you before it runs, and a scheduled run takes only the actions it was set up to take, within what the connectors allow. A blocked tool is therefore the dependable way to stop an action. Skill text is the place for conventions, such as what a call note must contain.

          What you do not configure here

          Stage names, field names and picklists are read live from your CRM. Change them in the CRM, and the skills follow.

          How to configure it, in four phases

          Connect your tools, point Claude at your source documents and ask it to customize the plugin. Claude reads the plugin and your tools, asks about what it cannot find, edits the skills, and hands back a plugin to review and install.

          Menu names here are as of mid-November 2026, and Anthropic is renaming some of them.

          Phase 1: Set up

          Who: each person. On Team and Enterprise plans, an admin enables the connectors first.

          1. Install the Sales plugin. Open "Plugins" in the left sidebar, find Sales and select "Add". Some organizations still see the older sidebar name, "Customize".
          2. Connect the tools you sell with. Connect the CRM first, then email, then calendar. That is the order the plugin's setup skill follows. Salesforce and Microsoft 365 need an admin to enable them before anyone can sign in.
          3. Run setup. Say "set me up". The skill shows what is connected, infers your role from the CRM and builds a starter dashboard. It also learns your writing voice from sent mail and recommends three skills to start with.

          Setup saves nothing by itself. It offers a short voice summary for you to keep in your project instructions.

          Phase 2: Configure

          Who: the operator who owns the sales process. A seller can do it for a copy of their own.

          1. Gather your sources of truth. Collect the documents where sales decisions already live: ICP, messaging, stage definitions, qualification method and brand guide. Put them where Claude can read them, or attach them.
          2. Ask Claude to customize the plugin. Open the installed plugin, select "Customize", then "Let's go". Claude reads the plugin and your connected tools, confirms what it found and asks about gaps.
          3. Review what comes back. Claude returns a summary of what it learned and a plugin card. Open the skills you will use every day and read them. Then select "Save plugin".

          Phase 3: Control

          Who: the admin for permissions. Each person for their own schedules.

          1. Set tool permissions. Each connector tool can be set to "Always allow", "Needs approval" or "Blocked". A sound start is reads allowed, with sends, posts and CRM writes on approval. On Team and Enterprise plans, owners set this for the whole organization.
          2. Schedule the routines. The setup skill offers four: a daily briefing, a CRM hygiene check, an end-of-day close-out and a weekly wrap. Create them from "Scheduled", then "New task".
          3. Decide what a scheduled run may do. The plugin's README advises keeping send, post and write tools on approval for scheduled runs. By design, a scheduled run takes only the actions you set it up to take. Anything else it finds becomes a proposal in its output.

          Phase 4: Share and maintain

          Who: the operator publishes. The admin sets who receives it.

          1. Roll it out. Anthropic's tutorial lists three routes: send the plugin file, host it in a Git repository set up as a marketplace, or have an admin add it for the organization.
          2. Choose how people get it. Organization owners set each plugin as available to install, installed by default, required or not available. Enterprise admins can vary that by group.
          3. Keep it current. When a source document changes, tell Claude what changed and save the plugin again. A plugin shared directly updates for its recipients. One published to the organization must be published again.

          A prompt to start from

          Customize the Sales plugin for my company.
Our sources of truth are the documents in [folder or links].
Use only what those documents and our connected tools say.
Where something is undecided, list it as an open question. Do not fill it in.
Do not copy prices, customer names or email addresses into the plugin.
Do not rename the plugin or any skill.
When you finish, show what changed in each skill and what you could not find.

          You do not need to cover everything in one session. Come back, tell Claude what to add and save again.

          If your organization already distributes the Sales plugin, members cannot edit that managed copy. Its owner should run the customization.

          In Claude Code

          The plugin's README gives two commands for Claude Code. Plugins saved to your Claude account also sync there when you sign in with that account.

          Do one or the other. A copy you install from the marketplace loads in place of a same-named plugin synced from your account, so the stock plugin would stand in for your company's configured build.

          claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins
claude plugin install sales@knowledge-work-plugins

          Short on time?

          1. Connect the CRM and email, then run setup.
          2. Paste your ICP and stage definitions into your project instructions.
          3. Customize the plugin when you want the setup shared.

          Three rules for what goes in

          • Write decisions, not aspirations. If the team does not follow a stage definition, the plugin will enforce a fiction.
          • Point to anything that changes often. For prices and quotas, name the document or field that holds the current figure.
          • Leave out anything sensitive. A shared plugin should hold no customer names, personal email addresses or credentials.

          Tips from a real configuration

          These tips come from one real configuration of the stock plugin. The worked example further down gives its numbers.

          Before you start

          • Point Claude at documents, not memory.Give it the files where decisions already live. It can then quote them and link back to them.
          • Name one owner.That person reviews the changes and answers the open questions.
          • Say what to ignore.Name the test records, sample data and internal accounts in your CRM. Otherwise they show up in pipeline reviews.

          While configuring

          • Give each skill only the facts it uses.In the real build, every skill got a short company section assembled from shared blocks. A call-prep skill does not need routing rules.
          • Keep one reference page inside the plugin.It holds every fact, a link to each source document and the list of open decisions.
          • Label how sure each fact is.The real build marked facts as recorded, observed or open. Recorded means written policy, observed means seen in the data, and open means undecided.
          • Never let the configuration invent policy.The company had no agreed stage exit criteria. The build kept a proposed mapping on the open list, switched off until the owner approves it.
          • Encode your wording rules.List banned words, required phrases and claims you cannot make. They then apply to every draft.
          • Separate what exists from what is planned.List shipped capabilities apart from the roadmap, so no draft sells the roadmap as built.
          • Replace vendor-specific passages.A few stock passages describe one vendor's mechanics, such as a CRM audit query. Swap in your own tool's equivalent.
          • Trim the connector list.The stock plugin lists 23 tool servers. The real build kept four and added the meeting recorder in use.
          • Keep every name.Do not rename the plugin or its skills. People, saved prompts and schedules call them by name.

          After configuring

          • Watch skill length.Every added paragraph is read on every run. The real build grew the skills' total word count by about 60 percent, and seven skills passed 3,000 words. Claude's own plugin-authoring guidance suggests staying under about 3,000 words per skill.
          • Check it like a contract.Ask for a before-and-after of each skill. Search the finished plugin for every banned word. Confirm skill names and the shared rules are unchanged.
          • Ask what is still missing.End by asking which company facts Claude could not find. That list is your next session.
          • Start with drafts.Keep sends, posts and CRM writes on approval until you trust the output.
          • Do not overread small samples.The setup skill will not guess a voice from fewer than five sent emails. Let company wording rules outrank a learned personal habit.

          Pitfalls to avoid

          Most configuration mistakes come from writing down too much, or writing down what nobody decided.

          PitfallWhat goes wrongDo this instead
          Hardcoding prices and quotasThey go stale and still get quotedName the document or field that holds the current figure
          Filling gaps with "industry standard"Skills enforce rules nobody approvedMark the gap as open and ask the owner
          Configuring before the process is decidedThe plugin repeats the confusionDecide stages and qualification first, or mark them open
          One seller's voice in a shared pluginEveryone's email sounds like that personKeep voice in each person's own instructions
          Renaming skillsSaved prompts, schedules and habits stop matchingKeep the names and change the content
          Allowing every write on day oneCRM changes and sent email that nobody reviewedAllow reads, and keep writes on approval
          Cutting the shared rulesSkills lose the rule that outside content is information, not instructionsLeave each skill's rules block as it is
          Putting every fact in every skillLong skills and diluted instructionsGive each skill only what it uses
          Forking by job titleBuilds drift apartKeep one build unless two teams truly sell differently
          Setting it up once and leaving itThe plugin and the documents disagreeName an owner, and update when a source changes
          Scheduling without deciding approvalsA run either waits for you or acts unreviewedChoose the task's approval mode on purpose
          Keeping a private copy beside the company buildTwo plugins share one name. In Claude Code, a copy you installed yourself loads in place of the one synced from your companyOne Sales plugin per person. Retire the private copy when the company build arrives

          A worked example

          This is one real configuration, built on November 15, 2026 for an early-stage B2B software company with a single seller. The company is left unnamed.

          What Claude found

          One CRM on its default pipeline, work email and calendar, a shared document drive and a meeting recorder. No team chat, enrichment tool or sales-engagement tool. The sales decisions lived in 15 documents, including a messaging framework, ICP and personas, the offer and its terms, and a brand guide.

          What changed

          Every skill gained a company section, built from 12 shared blocks plus notes written for that skill. Each skill's tool table now names the tools in use, and its opening step reads company facts instead of asking for them. Six skills had whole passages rewritten for those tools. Five more had smaller edits.

          What stayed out

          No prices, prospect names or email addresses were copied into the plugin. No stage exit criteria were invented: a proposed mapping waits on the owner's approval. Skill names, descriptions and the shared rules block are identical to stock.

          How it was checked

          Every skill was compared with its original, line by line. The finished package was searched for banned words. Names, descriptions and rules were confirmed unchanged.

          What is still open

          Four decisions went back to the owner: the proposed stage mapping, what amount a deal should carry, where prospect documents are saved and whether to finish CRM onboarding.

          The plugin was built and checked the day before this guide was written. It has not been in use long enough to report results.

          Questions people ask

          Do I have to configure it before using it?
          No. Every skill works with nothing connected, from uploaded files or pasted notes. It asks for what it needs.
          Do I need to be technical?
          No. Customizing is a conversation with Claude. A plugin is a folder of plain-text instruction files, and you can open any of them.
          Which plans include plugins?
          Anthropic's help center lists plugins on its paid plans. Sharing a plugin with colleagues and publishing one to an organization need a Team or Enterprise plan.
          Which CRM does it need?
          Any CRM with a connector. The plugin includes HubSpot, Salesforce, Close and Monday, and it reads your CRM's own stages and fields. With no CRM connected, upload a pipeline export.
          Will it send email or change the CRM by itself?
          It acts when you ask, within each connector's permissions. When a skill proposes a change you did not ask for, it shows the change and its evidence first. A scheduled run is different: it takes the sends and writes it was set up to take, within what the connectors allow and with no one there to ask. It carries out nothing that an email or a transcript asks for, and nothing whose recipient, target or content one of them dictates. For scheduled runs the plugin's README advises setting every tool that sends, posts or writes to ask first.
          I am a seller. Should I configure it myself or wait for my company?
          Look first for a Sales plugin your organization provides. If there is one, use it and add only your voice, role and schedules. If not, put your own facts in project instructions, and pass what works to whoever owns the sales process.
          Who has to be involved on a Team or Enterprise plan?
          Three seats. The admin enables connectors and sets permissions and availability. The operator writes the company facts. Each seller signs in and keeps their own voice and schedules. The section on who changes what covers each.
          Can different roles get different setups?
          One build serves every role. Personal details stay with each person, and Enterprise admins can set plugin access by group.
          Can my team edit the shared plugin?
          No. Members cannot edit a plugin the organization manages, or one a colleague shared with them. Changes go through its owner.
          What happens when Anthropic updates the stock plugin?
          Do not assume your customized copy picks up the changes. Plan to re-apply your configuration to a new stock version. A single reference page of company facts makes that quick.
          Does it work in Claude Code?
          Yes. The README gives install commands, and plugins saved to your account sync to Claude Code when you sign in.
          Where do I start if I am short on time?
          Connect the CRM and email, then run setup. Next, paste your ICP and stage definitions into your project instructions. Customize the plugin when you want the setup shared.

          crm-autopilotKeeps the CRM current from email, calendar and call transcripts.
          grow-pipelineChains prospect finding, outreach and CRM logging, with an approval at each handoff.
          growth-pulseShows whether sales and marketing are working, and ends with three actions for the week.
          reactivateFinds customers who have gone quiet and drafts a win-back message for each.
          proposal-builderTurns call notes, site photos or a request for proposal into a costed proposal.
          review-reputationGathers reviews and complaints into themes and drafts a reply to each review.
          ticket-deflectorReads a customer's email, checks order and account history and drafts a reply.
          ad-managerReads paid-ad results, recommends changes and makes the ones the owner approves.
          content-strategyUses sales data to plan 30 days of what to promote.
          social-content-engineKeeps a rolling posting calendar, writes captions and stages posts for approval.
          canva-creatorCarries out an approved campaign brief: calendar, designs, captions and staged posts.
          marketing-mondayA weekly growth briefing on results, customer comments and competitors.
          seo-ai-visibilityAudits how a site is found in search and in AI answers, and fixes what it can.

          The other 26 workflows cover finance, hiring, stock and setup: ap-processor, brand-style, build-agent, build-connector, business-pulse, cash-flow-snapshot, close-month, contract-review, grant-rfp-writer, hiring-screener, inbox-manager, inventory-planner, invoice-chase, job-post-builder, monday-brief, month-end-prep, pay-the-bills, payroll-prep, plan-payroll, report-builder, report-pack, restock, smb-onboard, smb-router, tax-prep and tax-season-organizer.

          Only the descriptions were read. What a skill can change, which tools it needs and who it suits are not set out here, and nothing is rated. The plugin's files are in Anthropic's public repository.

          ChatGPT for Sales, from OpenAI

          OpenAI, the AI lab that makes ChatGPT, is the vendor. Its Sales plugin gives ChatGPT 18 skills for sales work. This entry sets out what each one is reported to do, read and create, as ChatGPT read them from an installed copy.

          Browse the 18 skillsWhere these facts come from

          Preview. Reported by ChatGPT and checked by Claude. It awaits its editor's review.Sales plugin 1.1.7, read on November 22, 2026For revenue leaders and operators

          Where these facts come from

          The plugin's files are not public, so this entry rests on a report and says so. Read it as one relay of what the plugin's own text says it does, not as a test of what it does.

          Who read the plugin

          ChatGPT, an OpenAI model, in the editor's own account with the plugin installed. On November 22, 2026 it was given a fixed prompt that asked for an inventory of the plugin's own text and nothing else. It reported version 1.1.7, 18 skills and the full instructions of each. It ran no skill and called no connected app.

          How the report was checked

          By Claude, an Anthropic model. The prompt held back two facts from OpenAI's public page as a test: the count of skills and eight of their names. The report matched both. Every cross-reference between skills resolves to one of the 18, and what it says of publisher, capabilities and how to call the plugin agrees with OpenAI's pages, opened again on November 22, 2026.

          What that does not show

          We did not read the files, so a detail may be wrong or missing. No workflow was run, so nothing here says how well one works. The wording is ours: the plugin is quoted once, for its first prompt. Our own additions are marked: the grouping, who a skill is for, its GTM job and each example request.

          At a glance

          Provider and offering

          OpenAI, a vendor. ChatGPT for Sales was announced on November 17, 2026. It joins a Sales plugin built by OpenAI with more than 30 new or enhanced partner plugins. The copy read for this page is version 1.1.7.

          Category

          AI lab

          In one sentence

          A Sales plugin for ChatGPT with 18 skills, one that routes each request and 17 workflows, for researching accounts, preparing and following up meetings, planning deals, making the case to a buyer, reviewing a forecast and coaching reps.

          Go-to-market (GTM) jobs it covers
          • Lead qualificationenrich-company-and-contact-data
          • Account research and call preparationprepare-for-meetinganalyze-account-signalssales-company-researchfind-key-internal-sources
          • Outreach and follow-upfollow-up-after-call
          • Deal strategy and reviewsplan-deal-strategybuild-competitive-brief
          • Proposalsbuild-business-casesales-presentations
          • Pipeline review and forecastingreview-forecastseller-account-dashboardsales-leadership-dashboard
          • Coaching and enablementget-rep-call-feedbackreview-rep-call-trendsfind-customer-quotes

          Placed by us from the reported instructions. No skill of its own for CRM updates, onboarding and adoption, account planning and expansion, renewals, support, and daily planning: several workflows draft CRM text for review, and a renewal is handled as a deal or a meeting. Outside the list: index and demo-exec-and-seller-dash.

          Systems it works with

          The installed copy declares 46 optional integrations in 10 categories, from CRM and email to meeting transcripts and document signing. It does not record which are connected. The list.

          Who can get it

          OpenAI's help page says the Sales plugin is on every ChatGPT plan, the free one included. Partner plugins depend on plan, region and workspace settings, and installing Sales connects no partner account. The plugin's page says to use it in ChatGPT Work or in Codex. No price is stated.

          Controls

          Each workflow carries its own rules for what needs the user's say-so, and no workflow is reported to send a message or change a CRM record on its first pass. Admins of Business and Enterprise workspaces decide whether the plugin and partner plugins are available or installed, and review each app's access and allowed actions. The help page points to OpenAI's pages on security and compliance and does not itself say how customer data is kept or used.

          What the provider reports

          No measured result. The announcement carries statements from customers. One has a number: a co-founder at a customer company estimates about 65% less manual effort for some activities when HubSpot, a vendor's product, is used with ChatGPT for Sales.

          Evidence in the register

          None yet.

          Not public or not known

          The plugin's files are not public, and we have not read them. OpenAI's role-specific-plugins repository held only a placeholder note. Not known: whether each workflow behaves as its instructions say, since none was run. Also not known: which model runs a workflow, how any result is measured and the names behind 13 integrations that the installed copy stores as codes.

          On this site

          This entry. It rates nothing. Our read of fit, overlap and value, as the Claude Sales plugin entry gives it, waits for the workflows to be run.

          Last checked

          November 22, 2026: the installed copy through ChatGPT, and OpenAI's plugin page, help page and announcement by Claude.

          The 18 skills

          A user calls the plugin with @Sales and says what they want. One skill, index, reads the request and hands it to the workflow that fits. The other 17 are reached through it.

          • 7 of 18 describe a rerun on a schedule, and each asks before one is set up.
          • 5 of 18 can be run by a manager for a named seller.
          • 18 of 18 name a way to work from files or pasted text when no app is connected.
          • None is reported to send a message or change a CRM record on its first pass.

          The plugin sets no order for its skills. They are grouped here by the work they do, which is our read.
