          enrich-company-and-contact-dataFind and enrich companies and contactsSellers

          Completes the records you hand it, searches for companies or people who fit your criteria, or sorts a defined set into tiers and segments.

          Use it

          As ChatGPT reported the skill's instructions. The example request is ours and was not run.

          When
          Finding a buyer, identifying contacts, matching an ideal customer profile (ICP), completing missing fields, resolving duplicates, finding lookalikes or scanning a defined market signal. Not for meeting preparation, outreach to a known recipient or ranking a book you already own.
          Ask

          @Sales find 20 companies in [region] that match our ICP and the head of operations at each

          Give it
          A working set, or the criteria or seed companies to search from. Optional: a CSV or an export, domains, emails, the fields wanted, ICP rules, role, seniority, geography, size, technology, a ranking rule and a limit.
          You get
          A table of the completed records, a list of full and partial matches, or a table that compares, tiers or flags signals. Every row shows its evidence, how sure the match is and what stayed unresolved, with the sources and how much ground was covered.
          Reads
          Data providers for facts about companies and people, the technology they use, buying intent and similar companies. The CRM, to tell who is already known, owned or in a deal, and to catch duplicates. Your files for the ICP, target lists, territories and segment rules, and any rows you supply. Public sources only to confirm a point or fill a narrow gap.
          Can create or change
          Nothing at first. Afterwards it can export the table to a spreadsheet with its evidence and open questions intact. For the CRM it only proposes field changes: writing them is a separate action.
          Asks first
          Explicit approval before any search, export or enrichment that uses up provider credits, and before it touches personal contact data. A CRM update needs its own approval.
          Will not
          It does not invent contacts or fields, swap a data provider for broad web search or computer use, widen the scope quietly or claim to cover a whole market. It does not write to the CRM, create records or send outreach by itself.
          Whose work it covers
          A single company, a few contacts or a supplied list. It can also run one bounded search across a territory or a market.
          On a schedule
          Not stated.
          With no app connected
          It uses equivalent data you have already supplied and keeps to those companies and fields. If a provider is needed, it asks for the fewest fields that would let it check the filters.
          Company context it uses
          Your ICP and its hard limits, territories, segments, target lists, the conventions you follow when enriching records and any rule for ranking.
          Before and after
          Account prioritization or company research, as the next selling step.

          analyze-account-signalsWhat changed at an accountSellersCan be scheduled

          Tells you how a single account stands today, or sums up what has materially changed across a watchlist of limited size.

          Use it

          As ChatGPT reported the skill's instructions. The example request is ours and was not run.

          When
          A status check on a named account or a question about what changed there. Also a request for a digest of an owner's portfolio or of a watchlist. Ranking a whole book belongs to the seller dashboard skill.
          Ask

          @Sales what has changed at [account] in the last 14 days?

          Give it
          One identifiable company or CRM account. For monitoring: a watchlist, or an owner it can identify. Optional: the time window, which defaults to 14 days, focus areas and the style of the output.
          You get
          For one account: a snapshot, recent signals, an interpretation, recommended actions, open questions and missing evidence. For a watchlist: accounts ranked by material change, an action for each, details of the run and a plain statement where nothing much moved.
          Reads
          The CRM for who owns the account, its health and status, open deals and recent activity. Call transcripts for the customer's own words and decisions. Email for progress and requests left unanswered. Internal messages, account plans and notes for what the team knows. The calendar for meetings ahead.
          Can create or change
          Nothing: the readout changes no record. Follow-ups are CRM-ready updates drafted for review and an offer to set up a recurring monitor. A recurring run may not post a digest or write to the CRM by itself.
          Asks first
          No schedule until the user agrees. Tasks, posts, monitoring state kept elsewhere and CRM updates each need a separate request and approval.
          Will not
          It does not read a past change into a field's current value or manufacture a trend. Given a portfolio that is too large, it does not pick part of it at random. Monitoring never becomes CRM updates, tasks or posts made without the user.
          Whose work it covers
          A single account, or a watchlist of 50 accounts at most. An owner can be picked by ID or by email. Nothing is said about a manager's permission.
          On a schedule
          A daily or weekly rerun of the watchlist summary that only reads. It checks active and paused schedules for a duplicate first.
          With no app connected
          Complete records or an export that you supply. If it cannot establish the account or the change, it asks for the smallest missing identifier or piece of evidence.
          Company context it uses
          CRM ownership, territory, the portfolio or watchlist, account status and the focus areas a user defines.
          Before and after
          For a live deal: plan-deal-strategy. For a coming conversation: prepare-for-meeting.

          Points a seller to the colleague, document or channel that the evidence says is the right place to get a customer's question answered.

          It trusts documented ownership over a mention in chat, and owning an account in the CRM does not make someone the owner of an answer. It searches public channels unless the user asks for private ones and has access. It invents no people or links and escalates nothing by itself.

          One topic, question or support task, with or without an account.

          Not stated.

          Supplied documents, messages and what is already known. Where support is thin it names the smallest missing source and assigns no owner.

          Prepares one commercial meeting, lines up a day of them or builds a customer presentation out of the preparation.

A data provider where that adds something.

          It can put the brief into a meeting note you already keep or start a fresh document to read beforehand, offer to attach that to the invitation, draft a short update for chat or email, and build the deck from the brief once you have reviewed it. It can set up a schedule.

          It does not invent attendance, roles or checks of sources, and does not write scripts for facilitating the meeting. It respects a cut-off date. A recurring run may not attach notes, send messages or write to the CRM.

          Works from the record of a finished call to set out what was decided, who owes what and the follow-up to send, or a readout for the customer.

          find-customer-quotesFind what customers saidSellers

          Pulls customers' or prospects' exact words on a theme and shows the evidence for the words and for who said them.

          Use it

          As ChatGPT reported the skill's instructions. The example request is ours and was not run.

          When
          Voice-of-customer research, testing a theme, objections, product friction, evidence for a use case or quotations from named calls.
          Ask

          @Sales find customer quotes about onboarding time from last quarter's calls

          Give it
          A theme, an objection, a product area, a use case, a storyline or named calls, with evidence that keeps people's direct speech and who was speaking. Optional: a company, a segment, dates, calls and the number of quotes. The default target is five for each theme.
          You get
          Quotes grouped by theme, with the number found against the number wanted. Each quote names the speaker or company where known and gives a confidence score, a relevance score, the supporting evidence and its source. Gaps are listed and JSON is available on request. Anything said by a non-customer is labelled apart.
          Reads

          Nothing at first. The user can later ask for chosen quotes to be packaged.
          Asks first
          Posting, sending, packaging or saving quotes each wait for a later request from the user.
          Will not
          It does not polish, splice, paraphrase or invent a quotation. It wants confidence of at least 0.8 that the speaker is a customer or prospect, and relevance of 0.75 by default. It returns fewer quotes, or none, when the evidence is thin. It gives no legal or compliance approval.
          Whose work it covers
          Any number of themes, across the calls, accounts or segments you name.
          On a schedule
          Not stated.
          With no app connected
          The text of a transcript, an export from a recording tool that includes text or call notes that preserve what was said and by whom. With none of these it asks for the smallest usable source.
          Company context it uses
          Not stated. A company's CRM record, status and segment can filter the search.
          Before and after
          A business case, a competitive brief, meeting preparation or an evidence appendix can use the quotes. It can itself start from a recent call follow-up.

          A CRM update, a message, a recap or any further document each wait for a later request.
          Will not
          It keeps other deals at the same account out of the picture. It does not make up a buying committee, a stage, a price, a date, a security sign-off or a promise, and it marks roles and risks it has inferred as inferences.
          Whose work it covers
          One deal, renewal, negotiation or first sales motion. Use by a manager for a named seller is not stated.
          On a schedule
          Not stated.
          With no app connected
          Deal details that you supply, with the gaps marked. A first-sale plan needs no CRM, named customer, price or earlier discovery call.
          Company context it uses
          Account plans, CRM fields and any deal context supplied. No required sales method is stated.
          Before and after
          prepare-for-meeting when the request turns to meeting preparation.

          Builds the reasoning and evidence for a customer's investment decision, and puts numbers on value where the inputs support them.

          When
          A business case, a return-on-investment analysis, a value model, a pricing rationale, a review of a commercial proposal, a value story or a decision deck that needs new commercial analysis.
          Ask

          @Sales make the business case for [customer] to replace manual invoice matching

          Give it
          A customer, an account or a generic scenario, with a workflow, an initiative, a pain, a target metric or a decision. A case for a named customer needs authoritative account and commercial context. Optional: the buyer, industry, constraints, current tools, the solution, notes, metrics, usage, pricing, an earlier case, a template and the kind of output.

          A summary for executives, what the customer is trying to do and what stands in the way, the workflows and use cases that matter most, where value should come from, the metrics and assumptions, the return logic, what sets the offer apart, proof and caveats.           The CRM for the account, the deal, its contacts, stage, amount and timing. Call transcripts for the customer's pain, decisions and any numbers they gave. Your files for plans, earlier cases, proof and the account's metrics. A data provider to fill gaps. The company's own public material or filings where useful. Workbooks, proposals and templates you supply.
          Can create or change
          Only the output asked for, unshared: a decision document or a customer deck when one is requested. A suggested next step is a value-model table laid out for a spreadsheet.
          Asks first
          A request for a document or a deck authorizes that one item only. Otherwise the content is reviewed first, and saving or sharing needs an explicit request. It posts and sends nothing, leaves the CRM and your original template untouched, and creates no file you did not ask for.
          Will not
          It does not invent returns, prices, buyers, approval or evidence that a customer confirmed. Public or analogous proof is kept apart from the customer's own facts, and unsupported assumptions stay visible.
          Whose work it covers
          A single customer, initiative or buying decision, or a generic scenario. Use by a manager for a named seller is not stated.
          On a schedule
          Not stated.
          With no app connected
          Notes, metrics, links, exports or a generic scenario. Without credible numbers it returns a structural case and names the inputs a finance review would need.

          Commercial evidence for the account, proposal terms, customer metrics, proof points and templates.

          What it works with

          The installed copy declares 46 optional integrations, each a vendor's product. It does not record which of them an account has connected. Connecting an app, and what it may then reach, is settled with that app's provider.

          Category, as the plugin stores itEntriesNamed in the plugin's list
          Internal Messaging2Microsoft Teams, Slack
          Meeting Transcripts6Fireflies, Granola, Otter.ai, Zoom and 2 stored as codes
          CRM8Attio, Close, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zoho and 1 stored as a code
          Sales Intelligence10Actively, Apollo, Common Room, HG Insights, Meticulate, Rox, ZoomInfo and 3 stored as codes
          Email4Gmail, Outlook Email, Outreach and 1 stored as a code
          Knowledge & Files10Canva, Figma, Google Drive, Notion, SharePoint and 5 stored as codes
          Calendar2Google Calendar, Outlook Calendar
          Scheduling1Calendly
          Work Management1Monday.com
          Document Signing3DocuSign and 2 stored as codes

          13 of the 46 are stored as codes and not as names, and one of them sits in two categories. The plugin's README prints 40 names. Nine of those match no plain identifier: Agentforce Sales, Backstory, Clay, Gamma, Gong, Highspot, Salesloft, Seismic and Zoom Revenue Accelerator. Its files tie only Clay to a code, so the others are not placed in a category here.

          Three counts do not agree. OpenAI's page shows eight apps (Fireflies, Gong, Granola, Otter.ai, Slack, Teams, Zoom and Zoom Revenue Accelerator) and says there are 33 more, which makes 41. The README names 40. The installed copy declares 46. We could not reconcile them.

          Setup, company context and admin controls

          Install and connect

          From OpenAI's help page: open the Sales listing and install the plugin. Under "Works with", install the partner plugins you need, connect each with your own work account and review the permissions it asks for.

          From the installed copy: a workflow asks for a source only when it needs one. If the user declines, it asks for the smallest export, excerpt or file that would do, and stops only when a first result cannot be supported.

          First run

          The plugin's README gives a first prompt: @Sales Help me get started. The routing skill answers it with an introduction and offers the demo-exec-and-seller-dash. No separate skill for onboarding or company setup is stated.

          Company context

          No central settings screen and no company-wide intake is stated. Each workflow takes its context from records you give it or from sources it is allowed to read. For finding companies that means your ICP and territories. For a forecast, your stages and how you count amounts. For ranking accounts, your account plans and the rule for which accounts to leave alone. For research, the proof and messaging you have approved. For documents and decks, your templates.

          Customizing

          Dashboards, templates, reference inputs and some demo material can be customized, and a dashboard keeps its customizations when it is refreshed. A company's own connector can stand in for a source category. No way to edit, copy or extend the 18 skills is stated, and the plugin's manifest marks the package as proprietary.

          Admin controls

          From OpenAI's help page: in a Business or Enterprise workspace an admin opens the Admin Console, then Plugins, and sets the Sales plugin and partner plugins to available for installation or installed for the workspace. Admins also review each app's access, allowed actions and provider permissions. The installed copy states no control over single skills, over partner apps inside Sales or over single actions.

          An always-on agent

          OpenAI's announcement describes dot, an agent in ChatGPT that is always on and can use the same plugins. The installed copy describes schedules workflow by workflow and no single agent that runs them all.

          Before rollout

          From the plugin's own text, as reported

          • A request that only reads can still leave a file behind. seller-account-dashboard, sales-leadership-dashboard and build-competitive-brief do so as their normal result. A user who wants the competitive brief in the chat alone can ask for that.
          • Reading can still cost money. enrich-company-and-contact-data asks for approval before any search, export or enrichment that uses a data provider's credits, and before it touches personal contact data.
          • Different sources answer different questions. The CRM settles ownership, opportunity fields and the state of the forecast. Transcripts settle what a customer said and what was promised on a call. The calendar settles the details of an invitation.
          • Publishing a dashboard and scheduling its refresh are two approvals, not one.
          • The demo is fiction. It does not show that any provider is connected or can be written to.

          Our read Not from the plugin

          • Agree where the official number lives. The two dashboards and review-forecast give a second view of figures that a CRM or a forecasting tool already reports.
          • Decide who may spend provider credits before enrich-company-and-contact-data is in wide use.
          • Check your own rules for reviewing recorded calls before managers use get-rep-call-feedback and review-rep-call-trends on named reps.
          • Keep a person on anything a customer will see. Decks, business cases and follow-up emails are drafts until someone reviews them.

          Method, limits and sources

          The Claude Sales plugin entry was compiled from the plugin's own files, and the ratings in it are a first reading, which its editor has begun to change. The shorter plugin pages are described at the end.

          How it was put together

          • All 36 skill files, the README and the connector notes of Sales plugin 2.1.0 were read from an installed copy on November 21, 2026. A public copy sits in Anthropic's knowledge-work-plugins repository, under the Apache 2.0 license.
          • The tools a skill uses are taken by script from the table in its file. Whether a tool is read, or is somewhere the skill delivers to, was set by hand from that table's own words, and from the file's write line or a step where the table lists only a read. What a skill can change, send or post was written by hand from its file, and a script holds it to the file's own write line. Each skill that another one names was sorted by hand: one it hands work to, one it draws on or one it only mentions. The card leaves out the last kind. A script checks that each name shown is in the file. The build fails when the dataset and the files disagree.
          • What the build checks is narrow: that a skill named on a card is in that skill's file, that a tool's direction is one the table allows and that the four facts agree with the file's write line. It checks no number, no condition and no scope. Those rest on reading, and that is where all three rounds of outside checks found most of what they disputed.
          • Descriptions are restated in this entry's words. For the plugin's exact wording, open the skill file.
          • Each run card restates the skill's own trigger phrases, the inputs it names and what it accepts when no tool is connected. A request for a wider scope or for a schedule appears only where the skill's file takes one. The routines and their order are ours, and each link in one is checked against the file that states it.
          • On November 22, 2026 two models from other labs checked the entry's numbered claims against the plugin's files, in two rounds: an OpenAI model (GPT-6-based Codex, by its own account) and xAI's Grok Build. In the first round they disputed 78 of 398 claims between them. In the second they disputed 105 of the 595 claims of the corrected entry, much of it wording that the first corrections had added. Each round also held six false claims planted as a test, and each model caught all six both times. On November 23, 2026 the OpenAI model checked the 170 statements that had changed since, with five false ones planted among them, and caught all five. It disputed 52 of the entry's own. The most common fault, on 11 cards, was a line that read as a limit on what a skill can do, where every skill's file says an action you ask for goes through a connected tool. Claude checked each dispute against the file and made the corrections, and the editor decided what to accept. What they found and what changed is set out in kit/CROSSLAB.md. The text as it now stands has had no check from outside.
          • The configuration half is Nathan Fierley's guide, checked against the same plugin version on November 16, 2026. Its words are kept, apart from five small edits: three serial commas and one numeral changed to meet the site's style rules, and one sentence about buttons that this page replaced with a menu. Its sales leader is split here into a frontline manager and a leader. On November 22, 2026, 12 corrections were made here after the checks by two other labs' models, such as the number of skills written for leaders. Three of them were worded again on November 23, 2026, after the third check. Each change is listed in kit/CONFIGURE-EDITS.md. The guide's own published copy does not carry them yet.

          Fact and our read

          Three kinds of statement sit side by side in this entry. They are marked apart wherever they meet.

          • From the plugin's files. What each skill does, what it reads, what it can change, send or post and which skill it hands work to. The plugin is open source, so each statement can be checked against the skill files.
          • Our count from the files. Counts and groupings that we made from what the files say: the four markings of a skill's name, who takes a team or a named rep and which skills are named as routines. Each gives its rule, and none is a sentence in a file.
          • Our read. Which role a skill suits, where it overlaps a tool you may own, how much it is worth and how often it is used in a sales motion, when in the week it fits, the eight routines and their order, which model to start it on and what it leans on in your organization. The reasons are shown. None of it is usage data.

          Our read is a first reading by Claude, the AI model made by Anthropic, for Nathan Fierley to edit. He has changed parts of it, as the credits say. Anthropic also makes the plugin, so weigh the ratings with that in mind.

          The ratings place this plugin's skills against roles and sales motions. They do not score the provider, and they are kept out of the evidence register.

          What it does not tell you

          • How the skills perform in your business. One small test ran six skills from invented files, and it is described below. Nothing was run against a live CRM, and no time saved or deals won are claimed.
          • How often anyone uses a skill. The frequency ratings are estimates from how each skill is designed. Five skills are given an occasion in place of a frequency. Seven are named as routines in the plugin's files: daily-briefing, end-of-day, weekly-wrap, route-lead, deal-signals, competitive-intelligence and crm-hygiene-check.
          • How it compares. Only Anthropic's Sales plugin is covered in depth. The ChatGPT for Sales page sets out what OpenAI makes public about its own, and neither is rated against the other.
          • What changes next. Skills are added and reworded between versions. Check the version in this entry against yours.

          How the model test was run

          • What ran. Six skills, each on four Claude models, once: pipeline-review, crm-hygiene-check, forecast, call-summary, inbox-sweep and lead-triage. Each run was a fresh session that read the skill's file and followed it for one request, working only from the test files.
          • Where. In the agent harness this entry was built in, on November 21, 2026. That is not the Claude app, and nothing was connected. Effort was left at each model's default, which differs between models.
          • The answer key. The pipeline figures in the key were computed by script from the test file. The planted items in the call, the inbox and the leads were written with the files. One of those items was wrong: the key expected a draft reply to legal redlines, where the skill's file says to flag legal mail and not draft it. It was corrected on November 22, 2026, after a model from another lab caught it. Claude set the corrected mark on reading each reply again. The two markers did not mark it.
          • The marking. Two separate Claude sessions, one on Opus 5.5 and one on Sonnet 5.5, marked the four replies for each skill against the key, under code names. On that first marking they agreed on 390 of 396 marks. One guardrail mark was set on a second reading, and the reason is recorded with the files. So Anthropic models marked Anthropic models, on an Anthropic plugin. The key is made of facts that can be checked, and every reply and mark is published with this page.
          • What it is not. One run for each skill and model cannot separate a model's ability from chance. The test covers the from-files path only. It is our own test, and it stays out of the evidence register.

          How the other plugin pages were put together

          • Anthropic's plugins were read from a copy of its public repository at the commit of November 19, 2026. Each plugin's version and each skill's name and description were taken by script, and the build checks every name and count on these pages against them.
          • A skill list restates each skill's own description. The steps inside the skill files were read only for the Sales plugin.
          • The ChatGPT for Sales entry rests on a report, because the plugin's files are not public. On November 22, 2026 the site's editor installed the plugin in his own ChatGPT account and gave ChatGPT a fixed prompt, kept in this page's files, that asked for a read-only inventory of the plugin's own text. ChatGPT reported version 1.1.7 and the full instructions of 18 skills. Claude checked the report against two facts the prompt had held back, against itself and against OpenAI's plugin page, help page, announcement and plugins guide, opened on November 22, 2026. The entry restates the report in this site's words and quotes the plugin once. No workflow was run, and nothing in the entry is rated.
          • What ChatGPT marked as its own inference is not given as fact: the plan and mode of the session, the order of the skills and the names behind integrations stored as codes.
          • Which skills count as leader skills, and who may reach for each, is our read. The note on Google rests on one search and on its Workspace Updates post about skills. The note on Microsoft rests on its documentation of the sales skills in Copilot Cowork and on its post of November 17, 2026, both read on November 23, 2026. How the 18 skills divide between its two plugins is our count from the table in that documentation.
          • Nothing on those pages is rated, and none of their skills was run.

          Rules this entry follows

          • A listing is never paid for. Providers cannot pay to be listed, moved or described differently, and a listing is not an endorsement.
          • The provider's statements are dated. What this entry says about the product comes from the provider's own files and pages, with the date each was read.
          • Named systems only. Vendor names appear only where the plugin's own connector list gives them. Every other tool is named as a category.
          • The conflict is stated. This entry was compiled with Claude, an Anthropic model, and it covers an Anthropic product. On November 22, 2026 models from two other labs checked it against the plugin's files in two rounds, and on November 23, 2026 one of them checked what had changed since. Claude made the corrections after each. Before it is published it still needs its editor's review, and the latest corrections have had no check from outside.
          • One template. ChatGPT for Sales from OpenAI, also an AI lab and a vendor, is set out on the same 12 fields.
